Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

harnessr 0.7.0

harnessr 0.7.0 is the first release under the name harnessr. It reframes readgpt as a harness for model calls (clients, limits, a response cache, replay, traces and evaluation) with the document layer built on it. The sections below start with the changes that break code written for readgpt 0.6.0 or change its results, then the new features, then fixes and documentation. vignette("migrate") lists what to change in your code.

The package is now called harnessr

  • The package is now called harnessr. readgpt grew a general core for model calls (clients, spending limits, a response cache, recordings that replay offline, traces) under its document-reading layer, and the new name says so. Load it with library(harnessr). The GitHub repository is renamed to elkronos/harnessr too, and GitHub sends the old address there, so remotes::install_github("elkronos/harnessr") installs it and the old elkronos/readgpt still works. The website moves to https://elkronos.github.io/harnessr/. The core functions that began with gr_ now begin with hr_ (see “Renamed core functions”). Classes, arguments and prompts keep their names.

  • readgpt_example() is now gr_example(), which returns the same path to the bundled example document. The old name is removed (see “Removed”).

  • Requests, cache keys and recordings are unchanged by the rename. Every request is sent as 0.6.0 sent it, and the corpus store key is the one 0.6.0 computed. The response-cache and replay keys change in this release (see “Cache and replay keys” below), and the keys 0.6.0 computed are still looked up, so a warm cache, a recording made for hr_replay_client() and a gr_read_many() store all keep answering.

  • Two options are renamed: readgpt.api_key is now harnessr.api_key, and readgpt.allow_local_urls is now harnessr.allow_local_urls. The old names are no longer read (see “Removed”).

  • The help pages now suggest tools::R_user_dir("harnessr", "cache") for a cache that lasts. With that directory set, entries readgpt kept in tools::R_user_dir("readgpt", "cache") are read too, after it; new entries are written only to the new directory, and the old one is never cleared. The per-session default is now file.path(tempdir(), "harnessr-cache").

  • Text that named the package now says harnessr: the URL fetcher’s user agent (harnessr/<version>), the audit report’s title and footer, messages, and the Shiny app’s title. A trace’s meta still records the version under readgpt, so traces written before and after the rename read the same way.

Renamed core functions

The 27 core functions that still began with gr_ now begin with hr_, like the rest of the core layer. Document-layer functions such as gr_read() and gr_extract() keep gr_.

gr_backend_client() hr_backend_client()
gr_budget() hr_budget()
gr_cache() hr_cache()
gr_cache_clear() hr_cache_clear()
gr_cache_client() hr_cache_client()
gr_cache_stats() hr_cache_stats()
gr_call() hr_call()
gr_client() hr_client()
gr_count_tokens() hr_count_tokens()
gr_ellmer_client() hr_ellmer_client()
gr_embed() hr_embed()
gr_estimate_cost() hr_estimate_cost()
gr_mock_client() hr_mock_client()
gr_model_info() hr_model_info()
gr_model_limits() hr_model_limits()
gr_models() hr_models()
gr_options() hr_options()
gr_register_model() hr_register_model()
gr_replay_client() hr_replay_client()
gr_set_tokenizer() hr_set_tokenizer()
gr_tokenizer() hr_tokenizer()
gr_trace() hr_trace()
gr_trace_cost() hr_trace_cost()
gr_trace_save() hr_trace_save()
gr_trace_summary() hr_trace_summary()
gr_truncate_tokens() hr_truncate_tokens()
  • The old names are gone, with no alias, so a script that calls gr_call() stops with “could not find function”.
  • Class names and condition classes keep gr_: inherits(hr_mock_client(f), "gr_mock_client") is TRUE, and a handler for gr_call_cap catches the same condition as before.
  • Caches, traces saved with hr_trace_save(), replay cassettes and signal calibrations written by earlier versions still load.

Removed

The v1 functions (answer_question(), parse_text() and the gpt_read_*() family) are removed. Each one warned in 0.6.0 and pointed to its replacement; calling one now is an error. readgpt_example() and the options readgpt.api_key and readgpt.allow_local_urls go with the rename and had no deprecation period: the old function no longer exists, and harnessr ignores the old options. Caches, recordings and stores written before the rename still read: the readgpt-cache-v2 and readgpt-replay-v1 keys and the cache directory tools::R_user_dir("readgpt", "cache") are still looked up, and the corpus store key is computed as before.

Removed Use instead
answer_question() answer_document(), or gr_compare() for several recipes
parse_text() gr_ingest(), then gr_segment()
gpt_read_chunked() gr_read() with reader = "map_reduce"
gpt_read_retrieval() gr_read() with reader = "skim"
gpt_read_hierarchical() gr_read() with reader = "hierarchical"
gpt_read_multipass() gr_read() with reader = "ensemble"
readgpt_example() gr_example()
options(readgpt.api_key =) options(harnessr.api_key =)
options(readgpt.allow_local_urls =) options(harnessr.allow_local_urls =)
the gr_deprecated warning class none: nothing warns about an old name now

Built-in models carry limits and no prices

Providers change prices more often than harnessr is released, so harnessr no longer ships them. You set the prices you pay.

  • The built-in models now come from inst/extdata/models.csv: context window, output cap, kind, reasoning, temperature support and embedding dimensions, checked as of 2026-08. Their limits are unchanged. Their input_usd and output_usd are NA, so hr_estimate_cost() returns NA for them until you set prices, and under a max_cost_usd limit a request to one is sent with a warning (below).
  • New hr_load_models(file) registers models from a CSV file. A row may name a built-in model and give only input_usd, output_usd and as_of: the model keeps its limits and gains the prices. A malformed file stops with an error of class hr_bad_models_file naming the row and column, and registers nothing. ?hr_load_models documents the format.
  • hr_register_model() prices a known model without its limits: hr_register_model("gpt-4o", input_usd = 2.5, output_usd = 10) keeps gpt-4o’s context window, output cap and other fields. Leaving out either limit changes the current entry and keeps every value you leave out. A call that gives both limits works as before.
  • A built-in models file that cannot be read stops the package from loading, with an error of class hr_bad_models_file, instead of leaving the registry empty.
  • New option allow_unpriced (TRUE). Under a spending limit, a request to a chat model with no price is sent, as in 0.6.0. The trace prices it NA, and the first such request to each model in a session warns with class hr_unpriced_model that the spending limit does not cover the model until you set its prices. Token and call limits still apply: set max_tokens_total to bound such a run. A read gives this warning before it starts, and no longer adds a gr_cost_uncheckable warning on every run. hr_options(allow_unpriced = FALSE) or hr_governor(allow_unpriced = FALSE) refuses such a request instead, with a condition of class hr_unpriced_model, and gr_read() then stops before its first request. hr_mock_client(), replays and embedding models with no price are never refused or warned about. An ellmer chat is priced as the model it was built with, whatever a spec names. With parallel = TRUE the workers do not repeat this warning or the stale price warning, and it names the limit you set, not a worker’s share.
  • New option price_max_age_days (120). A cost computed from prices older than that, counted from the first day of their as_of month, warns with class hr_stale_price, once per model per session. NULL turns the warning off. Set the current prices again to clear it.
  • To set prices, call hr_register_model(id, input_usd =, output_usd =) for one model, or keep a CSV file of prices with an as_of column and load it with hr_load_models() at the top of each script. “Prices” in vignette("models") walks through both, checking prices with hr_models(), unpriced models and stale prices. vignette("migrate") lists what changes for code written for 0.6.0. The guides, the README and the examples set illustrative prices before they show a cost.

Cache and replay keys

  • hr_call() takes a draw_index for the draws of a sampled request: 0, the default, for an ordinary call, and 1, 2, … for repeated draws. Above 0 it is part of the response-cache key, so N identical calls with draw indexes 1 to N are N cached replies; before, a cache returned the first reply N times and anything that compared them saw perfect agreement. A handler finds it in params$draw_index and the trace records it in the step’s params; at 0 neither carries it, so an ordinary call is unchanged.

  • Stages send their requests at their trace’s draw. gr_claims(), gr_outline(), gr_synthesise() and gr_read_many() each record on a trace of their own and send their requests at the draw index and draw scope of the trace they are given, and the items of a parallel batch carry the run’s draw index and scope the same way, so under an hr_cache() each run of a benchmark gets its own replies. Requests made without a draw index are unchanged, and so are their cache keys. A recording made without per-draw keys is answered, for a later draw, with its replies in recorded order.

  • The response-cache key is now harnessr-cache-v3, a SHA-256 hash (64 hex digits) in place of xxhash64. Entries written under the old key (readgpt-cache-v2, by readgpt 0.6.0 and earlier builds of harnessr) are still read for calls with no draw index: a call that finds nothing under its new key is looked up under the old one. The first reply found that way in a session warns once for the cache, with class hr_legacy_key, and hr_cache_stats() has a new column, legacy_hits, that counts them. Old entries are never rewritten, new ones are written under the new key only, and hr_cache_clear() removes both.

  • The replay key is now harnessr-replay-v2, and covers the temperature (once the session default is filled in), the output cap asked for and the JSON schema as well as the messages, model and effort. A replay under another temperature, cap or schema now misses instead of being answered with the recorded replies. Each model step of a trace records its key as replay_key. A step recorded before that is looked up by the old key (readgpt-replay-v1: messages, model and effort), with one hr_legacy_key warning per recording in a session and a count in $stats()$legacy_hits. A replay’s own trace records a reply found that way, or one repeated under on_exhausted = "flag", without a replay_key, so a replay of that trace still goes through the old key, or still runs out of replies. A miss on a prompt recorded for the model at the effort asked for says the temperature, output cap or schema differ, names the recorded settings next to the ones this call asks for, and says which of them differ. Where the schema differs, the recorded cap is given as the cap that was sent, which may be the model’s limit rather than the cap asked for.

  • A replay that runs out of recorded replies is an error. A call past the last reply recorded for its request, or for a draw that was never recorded, raises hr_replay_exhausted. It used to repeat the last reply, so a replay making more calls than the recorded run looked like an exact reproduction. hr_replay_client(on_exhausted = "flag") keeps the old behaviour, counted in $stats()$repeats. A call with a draw_index above 0 is answered with the reply recorded for that draw, or the k-th reply to the request in a recording made without draw indexes.

Other changes to requests and results at the default settings

Each change below alters what a run at the default settings sends or returns, so a cache or a recording made before it can miss, or a figure can move.

  • A JSON reply must fit the schema the request sent. Every call that asks for JSON (screening, claims, outlines, preview plans, rerank, iterative reading, model segmentation, extraction) now checks the reply’s types, enum values and required fields, through nested objects and arrays, before using it. A reply that fails is treated as a reply that did not parse: the reader takes its failure path, and the reply is not cached, so running again asks again. A cached reply that fails is asked again too. It used to be enough for a reply to be a named object, so {"decision": "probably"} was a screening reply and was stored as one. Some replies that used to be read leniently are now failed calls: a screening decision outside include, exclude and unclear (it was read as “unclear”), a text field sent as an array or object in iterative, rerank and gr_screen() (it was joined into one string), and a proposition list sent as an array of arrays (the batch is kept as written). Where a reader reports why a call failed, it now says where the reply broke the schema, as in $.groups[0]: expected array, got 1. gr_extract() still reads each field’s value itself, so “1,204” in an integer field is still 1204 and an undeclared value is still reported as one it could not read; only the shape of its replies is checked.

  • Comparing vectors of different lengths is an error. Cosine similarity cut both vectors to the shorter length, so a lexical fallback vector scored against an API embedding gave a plausible number from two unrelated spaces. It now stops with an error of class hr_dim_mismatch. The readers already kept the query and the chunks in one space; iterative now also falls back to word overlap for a round whose query came back with no vector.

  • gr_calibrate() computes kappa on kept against excluded. 0.6.0 took kappa over the screener’s three labels (include, unclear, exclude) against the person’s two, so every "unclear" counted as a disagreement, while sensitivity in the same object counted an unclear record as kept. The primary table is now kept (include or unclear) against excluded, the definition sensitivity uses, and $agreement$strict holds strict include against the rest as a secondary table. On the eight-record example in ?gr_calibrate kappa moves from 0.33 to 0.50. 0.6.0’s figure is no longer reported.

  • The references cleaner, in the "academic" and "legacy" presets, now cuts at a Markdown heading such as ## References or ### 7. References, with or without closing # marks, and not at a line inside a fenced code block, such as a # references comment. It matched only a line that held the word alone, so a Markdown document kept its reference list under both presets. The example report ends with ## References, so under "academic" it now sends 62 fewer prompt tokens than under "standard", not 26. The research and legacy recipes send shorter requests for such a document, and so do gr_screen() and gr_extract(), whose default recipe is research: at their defaults their requests and cache keys change for a Markdown document with a references heading in its last 60%, so a hr_cache() built before this misses for those documents. Requests under the "standard" preset, the default of answer_document(), do not change. The cleaner no longer cuts a Markdown file at a line indented four or more spaces (” # References”), which in Markdown is code, not a heading. PDF and plain text still allow any indent. gr_ingest() tells the cleaners what read the file in .source_type.

  • The claims and writing prompts now show each extracted value with its check and its quote, as n: 120 (verified quote: "We enrolled 120 people."), when they are given a gr_extract() result. This changes what is sent at the default settings: every claims and section request made from an extraction carries the quotes, so its cache and replay keys change and earlier cached replies for these requests are not reused. A bare table carries no quotes and is sent as before.

  • Claims are ranked by the certainty of their direction tally, not by how many studies vote. Each claim in gr_claims()$claims gains sign_p, the exact two-sided sign test of n_support of n_support + n_contradict studies, and low_power, TRUE for a tally of 5 studies or fewer, where no split can reach p < 0.05. Sections rank their claims by sign_p, lowest first, then by study weight, so a 5-of-5 claim now ranks above a contested 3-to-3 one. A claim that more of its studies contradict than support ranks after every other, the least contradicted first, since sign_p is two-sided and would rank 1 supporting and 8 contradicting (p = 0.039) above 5 of 5. print() gives each claim’s tally and p (5 of 5 prints p = 0.0625) and warns of low power, citing Campbell et al. 2020 (SWiM) and Boon and Thomson 2021; the audit report adds sign_p. This changes what is sent at the default settings for a section given claims in a different order: the claims block lists them, and assigns their sentence budgets, by the new rank.

  • gr_claims() gains moderators, last: the columns you expected, before reading, to explain a disagreement. Each moderator a claim names is now tested, in $moderators: declared (named in moderators) or exploratory (not declared, or one study against one), Fisher’s exact fisher_p of the split, min_p, the smallest p a split with those numbers of studies can give, and holm_p, Holm’s adjustment over the declared moderators. $claims gains moderator_status. print() and the audit report give the tests and list the ICEMAN items (Schandelmaier et al.

    1. to assess each moderator against; harnessr scores none of them. The writing prompt marks an exploratory moderator, distinguished by: design (exploratory), which changes what is sent at the default settings for a section whose claims name a moderator, since with no moderators declared every moderator is exploratory.

  • Claims reconciled across batches are no longer merged when they differ in direction, between findings, or in the population they name (adults, children, adolescents, infants, older people, women, men, students, from the claim and its scope), whatever the reconcile reply grouped; such a group is split, with a gr_claims_kept_apart warning and a note on each part. Direction is read from words on three axes: a null finding (“has no effect”, “did not improve”, “ineffective”, “unchanged”) against an effect, a benefit against a harm (“benefits”, “harms”), and a rise against a fall (“raises”, “reduces”). “Improves depressive symptoms” and “reduces depressive symptoms” stay together, and so “improves Y” and “reduces Y” are not told apart; a population outside the list is not recognised. A merged claim takes the wording of the member most studies support, then the one fewest contradict, then the first in a fixed order, instead of the longest, so the claims no longer depend on the order of the table. This changes what is sent at the default settings when claims come from more than one batch and the reconcile reply merges or groups them: the merged claim’s wording, and the number of claims where a group is split, feed the gr_outline() and gr_synthesise() prompts, so those requests, and their cache and replay keys, differ from before.

  • The blocks of a PDF page OCR read now have kind = "ocr" (headings keep "heading"), as the blocks OCR reads from a Word file’s images and from image files always had. This changes the blocks of a document at the default settings when tesseract and magick are installed and a page is OCR-ed: it is a fix, since the blocks did not say their text came from OCR, and no text and no request changes. Without tesseract nothing changes.

  • hr_options() given one named argument whose value is a list now sets that option. It used to read the list as a set of options to restore, which only an unnamed list should be.

  • An effort map that names no declared call is an error. A name in gr_read_spec(effort =) (and the effort of gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise()) must be a declared stem, a part of one up to a dot ("synthesise", "segment"), or a label under one ("reduce.level1"). Anything else stops with an error of class hr_unknown_effort_key that lists the stems. readgpt 0.6.0 accepted such a name and matched no call, so a misspelt c(extrac = "low") sent every extraction call at the provider’s default with nothing said. An effort map that names the calls of a reader or segmenter of your own needs that module registered first, with its labels in calls.

Limits checked before every request

  • max_calls and max_cost_usd now hold exactly. Every request is checked before it is sent, by the call path itself, against what the run has spent plus the most the request could cost: its prompt at the input price and its output cap (for a reasoning model, the raised cap hr_call() sends) at the output price. The prompt is counted with the JSON schema and extra body fields the request carries and a few tokens of framing per message, then raised by safety_margin, since the provider bills for all of that. A request that could take the run past a limit is not sent. Runs used to stop only once what they had spent reached the limit, so they ended up to one request over it; they now end at or under it, as long as the provider stops each reply at its cap and counts the prompt within that margin of the local tokenizer. A run that leaves its output caps at the model’s limit stops while it still has headroom a smaller cap would have used.

  • A refused request is not a call. It comes back from hr_call() as a failed result with refused = TRUE and an error naming the limit, after a condition of class hr_budget_refused is signalled (catch it to stop instead). It adds nothing to the trace’s calls, steps or spend; the trace lists it in a new refusals field, sets budget_stop and names the limit in stop_reason. Readers and review stages treat it as they treated reaching a limit before: the answer or section is marked partial, and the request is not counted as failed.

  • Every request is checked, not only the ones a reader asked about. Judges, the ensemble’s adjudication, conflict resolution in extract, context and proposition segmentation, claims, outlines, screening, synthesis and embeddings requests all go through the same check, as does any request a custom reader or a script makes with hr_call(). The readers no longer check trace_can_call() themselves. It is kept for custom readers written to the 0.6.0 help page, which still work.

  • New option max_tokens_total (NULL, off) limits the tokens a run may use: prompts and replies of every call, and text sent to be embedded. A request whose prompt and reply at its cap would pass it is refused with stop_reason "tokens". It is the limit that still bounds a run on an unpriced model under allow_unpriced = TRUE. gr_compare() holds the whole comparison to it, as it does to max_cost_usd.

  • New hr_governor() holds a run’s limits: max_calls, max_cost_usd, max_tokens_total, max_output_tokens (the largest output cap one request may carry; a request with a larger one is refused, not cut down), allowed_models and allow_unpriced. Attach one with the new hr_trace(governor = ) argument; a trace without one reads the limits from hr_options(), as before. The new limits are also options, max_tokens_total, max_output_tokens, allowed_models (all NULL, off) and allow_unpriced (TRUE), so every trace’s config snapshot now lists them. as_json() writes a trace’s refusals and governor when it has any, with allowed_models always as an array. gr_read_many(), gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise(), which keep a trace of their own and fold it into the one they are given, hold their requests to what that trace’s governor has left: the calls (every recorded request, cache hits and embeddings requests included), the dollars and the tokens. Without a governor, hr_options(max_calls =) is a limit per document for gr_read_many() and per stage for the others.

  • A parallel batch cannot pass a limit. Each worker’s items are held to an equal share of the calls and dollars the run has left, and an item its share refused before it sent anything runs again in the calling process, against the run. A batch that the run’s limits cannot cover still runs in the calling process, as before. Batch items make one request each; an item that made more and had a later one refused by its share warns (gr_parallel_share) and does not mark the run as stopped.

Traces record what was sent and what came back

  • Each request step records params_sent, the request as it went out with every default resolved: the model, api, base_url, the output cap actually sent (a reasoning model’s small cap goes out raised to 2048), the temperature (filled from hr_options("temperature"), or NA when none was sent), the effort, the schema name, and SHA-256 hashes of the schema and of the extra body fields. For a hr_client() it is read from the request body itself. params keeps what the caller asked for, as before. Requests, response-cache keys and replay keys are unchanged.

  • Steps record served_model, response_id and fingerprint where the provider returns them, beside model, which stays the model asked for and is what a step is priced and replayed by. None of them enters a cache or replay key. hr_call() results carry the same three fields.

  • Steps record attempts, the number of requests sent, retries included (0 for a reply from a cache or a recording), and started_utc and ended_utc as ISO 8601 in UTC with a trailing Z. A saved trace’s started is now written in UTC with a Z too; it was local time with no offset.

  • Token records say where they came from. A step’s tokens gains provenance: "reported" by the provider, "counted" here with the "tiktoken" tokenizer, or "estimated" with another one. Reasoning and cached input tokens the provider reports are kept as tokens$reasoning and tokens$cached_input, parts of output and input rather than additions. hr_trace_summary() gains tokens_reasoning, tokens_cached_in and usage_estimated, the share of requests whose counts were estimated, and print() on a trace says that share when it is above zero. A request that failed before the provider sent any usage records a "counted" zero, and a handler’s reply that gives no usage is counted here rather than taken as a reported 0 in and 0 out.

  • Embeddings requests record attempts, served_model and a provenance like any other request; attempts was always NA although they are retried, and a failed one had no provenance. as.data.frame() on a trace gains tokens_reasoning, tokens_cached_in and served_model columns when some request has them, and hr_trace_cost() gains paid_reasoning and paid_cached_in.

  • Cached input can be priced at its own rate. hr_register_model() takes cached_input_usd, hr_estimate_cost() takes cached_input_tokens, and hr_models() shows cached_input_usd_per_1m. A model with no cached rate prices cached input as other input, so a model you priced without one costs what it did before.

  • Runs record who they are for. hr_trace() takes system, owner, run_by, purpose and approved_by, and the new option hr_options(actor = list(...)) sets them for every trace; a field named nowhere is NA. They are written to a saved trace under actor and shown by print() when set.

  • Runs record the options in force when the trace was made, under config, with the R version. The values of api_headers are left out, since they can hold credentials.

  • refine and hierarchical write the length of the state they carry. Each refine.draft and refine.revise step in the trace gains state$tokens_in (the draft the request carried) and state$tokens_out (the draft carried on from it, which is the old one when the reply was unusable). Each hier.summarise.L<k> step gains the length of the text it summarised and of the summary it returned, the hier.answer step the length of the summaries it was sent, and each level adds a local hier.state.L<k> step with the number of summaries handed on and their combined length. A draft that shrinks sharply in one revision can now be seen in the trace.

  • Every cut writes a truncate step to the trace with where it was made (detail$where: refine.excerpt, refine.draft, hier.summaries, preview.skim, preview.outline, <label>.input for a finding cut to fit a merge, <label>.giveup for the capped findings a failed merge returns, segment.contextual.header, segment.contextual.document, screen.opening, synthesise.gaps, embed.input), the token limit, and the tokens before, kept and dropped (the truncation marker is not counted as kept). For screen.opening the limit is the screening cap on the opening with its heading; for segment.contextual.header it is the room the header was cut to. A preview.skim cut lists the cut section’s chunk_ids, always as a JSON array. refine and hierarchical answers also gain notes$tokens_truncated, and their printed answer now says how many tokens were cut (“N token(s) cut to fit”) when a cut happened. The preview reader’s notes$tokens_truncated is now the tokens a cut dropped rather than the overshoot over the cap, a correction to a count that measured the wrong thing. Requests, cache keys and replay keys are unchanged; the trace of a run that cut nothing gains only the state lengths above.

  • New gr_methods_text() writes a plain paragraph for a methods section from a result, a trace or a benchmark: the harnessr version, the models asked for and the models the provider said answered, request and run counts, the tokens sent (a request a cache or a recording answered sent none, and its recorded tokens are given apart), the settings changed from their defaults, and a hash of each system prompt by stage. It reads only the record and makes no claim beyond it.

Cost reports say where their prices came from

Every report of a cost in dollars now says, for each model it prices, whether the model has a price, the month of that price, and whether its registry entry is a fact or a guess. Existing columns and fields keep their names and meanings, and the new ones come after them (in gr_compare(), before premise, which stays last).

  • hr_trace_cost(), as.data.frame() on a trace and gr_compare()’s summary gain the columns priced, as_of and certain, and so do the new hr_benchmark() and the cost table of hr_effort_check(). hr_report()’s cost table has them per arm, and adds a note naming any arm with an unpriced model. hr_judge()’s judge_cost has the same fields and models. gr_inventory()’s totals gains them for its cost floor. gr_read_many()’s summary gains them after warnings (before premise), and the audit report’s corpus table shows them in a prices column.
  • hr_estimate_cost() gains detail. detail = TRUE returns a one-row data frame: model, usd, priced, as_of and certain. The default still returns the figure alone.
  • Printed costs give the month of their prices, as in $0.0021 across gpt-4o, prices as of 2026-11. A model with no price prints as “no price set for ”, with hr_register_model() and hr_load_models() named as the way to set one. A total over several models of which some have no price says that it covers the priced models only, where it used to print “cost unknown”. The data still hold NA for such a total. The progress line says “spent on priced models” in the same case. The audit report’s cost table has a prices column.

Context, effort and revision checks

Each option below is off by default, so a default spec sends the requests it sent before and keeps its store, cache and replay keys. Each new setting is declared with its evidence (untested), is listed by gr_settings_table(), and has a walkthrough that says how to test it with hr_sweep().

  • hr_truncate(text, n, keep) cuts text to n tokens and keeps the part asked for: the start ("head", the default, which is hr_truncate_tokens() itself), the end ("tail"), both ends ("both") or the units with the highest scores ("scored"). With a trace, a cut writes a "truncate" step naming the piece, the part dropped (dropped_part) and the tokens it held. hr_context_policy() states which pieces of a request are never cut (pin), which are cut first (cut_order) and which part of each is kept (keep), and hr_context_fit() applies one to a set of named pieces.

  • gr_read_spec() gains context_policy. With a policy, refine fits its state and the new excerpt into the input budget together instead of halving it; the merges of map_reduce and skim, hierarchical’s summaries and preview’s outline and skims are cut under the policy’s keep rule for their piece; and the readers that pack whole chunks (stuff, retrieve, rerank, iterative, preview’s re-read) write a "truncate" step naming the chunks they left out. Under order_merges = TRUE, the findings a merge combines and the answers ensemble adjudicates are placed by context_order. NULL, the default, keeps each reader’s cuts as they were.

  • gr_read_spec() gains refine_state. "ledger" makes refine carry a numbered list of findings: each request replies with edits (ADD, REPLACE n, DROP n) that the code applies, so a finding no edit names is kept word for word and a corrected one is replaced, and one more request, refine.answer, answers from the list. "draft", the default, rewrites the draft as before.

  • restate gains "window", which repeats the question once the excerpts pass the model’s effective window. No model’s window is measured yet, so it uses 50,000 tokens and warns (gr_window_unmeasured).

  • gr_condensation_check() builds a benchmark of what a reader keeps as it condenses a document: facts planted in a synthetic document or a text of your own, lures (the same measure for a near-namesake, with another value) and a fact stated wrongly early and corrected late, each document given forwards and reversed by paragraph (gr_reverse_text()). It returns an hr_reference() and a scorer that finds the values in the answer with no model judge, for hr_benchmark() to run arms that differ in refine_state, context_policy or the reader; and gr_condensation_summary() gives each arm’s fact recall, lure rate, whether the correction won and recall of the facts read last. The live comparison on real documents is not part of this release.

  • hr_effort_escalate() is an effort policy that starts every stage low and sends the next stage raised when a trigger fired in the one before: a cut, a reply stopped at its cap, a reply that is not the JSON asked for or does not fit its schema, a reply the caller names (such as NOT_IN_DOCUMENT from every request of a stage), or an event the caller reports with hr_effort_event(). Effort changes only at stage boundaries, at most max_escalations times a run. The stage after a raised one goes back to the base effort unless it fired a trigger too and a raise is left. A cut counts for the stage whose request it was made for. Each raise is an "effort.escalate" step of the trace and its outcome an "effort.resolve" step; hr_effort_log() lists them. hr_call() takes the policy as its effort.

  • gr_read_spec() gains effort_mode. "escalate" makes the read’s effort such a policy, starting at effort ("low" when unset) and raising to "high"; iterative reports a quotation it could not verify, ensemble members that disagree, and screening an unclear decision or draws that disagree. "static", the default, sends effort as before.

  • hr_effort_check() compares an effort policy’s arm with fixed-effort arms on a benchmark, with hr_report()’s non-inferiority test at a stated margin and Holm’s procedure over the comparisons, and reports each arm’s accuracy, cost, requests per run, raises and the requests sent raised. Without a registration from hr_register_contrasts() the contrasts are marked post hoc. It plans nothing: there is no effort planner.

  • gr_synthesise() gains revision_check. "judge" puts an advisory check behind the word-counting guard of the coherence passes: each sentence a kept revision changed is graded by hr_judge(), its requests held to the run’s limits, against the draft sentences it came from, as "holds", "stronger" or "not_entailed". A flagged sentence is warned about (gr_revision_flagged), counted in a flagged column of $coherence and listed in $revision_flags; the revision is kept as it was. “Is associated with” made “reduces” passes the word lists and is flagged by the judge; a hedge moved into another sentence is not. "lexicon", the default, sends no judge request.

Reading options

Each option below is off by default, so a default spec sends the requests it sent before and keeps its store, cache and replay keys. Each is declared with its evidence (untested unless a source is named), is listed by gr_settings_table(), and has a walkthrough in vignette("readers") that says what it trades off and how to test it with hr_sweep().

  • preview logs each section its plan skips as a preview.skip step in the trace, with the section’s BM25 score against the question. Two settings guard against a plan that skips the answer: unskip_k reads the k sections that match the question’s words best even when the plan skips them (notes$unskipped), and reread_on = "not_found" follows a NOT_IN_DOCUMENT answer with one request (preview.reread) over the sections not read in full (notes$reread).

  • rerank records notes$retrieval_low_score = TRUE, and a rerank.low_score trace step, when every candidate the model scored is below rerank_min_score; before, only the reason string said so. The new setting low_score = "read_top_k" sends the 5 best-scored candidates to the answer request in that case instead of answering NOT_IN_DOCUMENT unasked, and marks a NOT_IN_DOCUMENT reply with retrieval_low_score.

  • retrieve and iterative rank chunks through one fusion function. At fusion = "default" each keeps its 0.6.0 ranking (retrieve blends cosine with BM25 on lexical embeddings, iterative uses cosine), so the two give the same order on the same inputs whenever the embeddings are not lexical. fusion = "rrf" is reciprocal rank fusion of the cosine and BM25 rankings for both, with rrf_k = 60, the constant Cormack, Clarke and Buettcher (2009) use.

  • Every answer from gr_read() carries $outcome: "answered", "partial", "not_found", "refused" (a limit stopped the run) or "failed" (every model request it made failed, or the reader reports an error), for every reader. is_not_found() given an answer reads it, so a refused or failed run no longer counts as the document lacking the answer; given a string, or an answer without the field, it tests the sentinel as before. as_json() writes the field.

  • answer_format = "schema" sends the answering requests with a JSON schema holding answer and outcome, so the model reports a not-found in a field rather than with the sentinel; "parsed", the default, sends the free-text requests as before. The default stays until a live comparison of the two on the default model.

  • premise_verdict = "structured", with premise = TRUE, asks the answering requests for a premise_status field and the quote from the excerpts that contradicts the question, in a JSON schema, and checks the quote with the span matcher gr_verify_evidence() uses against what the request was shown (and the document, where that was text a model wrote, as in skim and hierarchical). The answer gains $premise_verdict. In map_reduce, a chunk’s flag whose quote is absent or not found in the chunk is dropped (notes$premise_dropped), and a verified one goes to the merge and sets notes$degradation to "premise_flagged". The default, "sentence", sends what premise = TRUE sent before.

  • gr_read_spec(verify = TRUE) checks an answer’s quotations against the chunks they come from and lets the check decide what is accepted. gr_read() runs gr_verify_evidence() on the answer, writes its columns onto $evidence, marks the answer partial when a quotation is not found (notes$unverified_evidence), notes how many it checked (notes$quotes_checked) and records a read.verify step in the trace. The iterative reader’s step must then list the passages its answer rests on, word for word with their chunk numbers, and the loop stops only when every one is found in the chunk it names, among those the step was shown. A refused step is told which quotations were not found; a run that ends with none accepted answers NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, keeps the refused answer in notes$unverified_answer and makes no final answer request. Its evidence is the quoted passages, not every chunk it was shown. A refusal is sent back even when retrieval has no unseen chunks left, so the next step can quote what it already has. With premise = TRUE, a step that reports the premise false is not held to quotations in this release and stops the loop as it does without verify. verify = FALSE, the default, sends every request as before, and the field is in the spec only when TRUE, so cache, replay and corpus store keys are unchanged.

  • A second quote matcher is recorded beside verified. Evidence tables that are checked (skim, extract, screen, iterative with verify = TRUE) and gr_verify_evidence() gain quote_status, quote_sim, quote_coverage, quote_edits and quote_critical_ok, from a matcher that expands ligatures, joins words broken across a line with a hyphen, undoes JSON escapes and scores the closest window of the source by character edits, with numbers (in digits or in words, with any comparison sign before them and the unit after), and negations required to be identical. A passage too long to score (its length times the source’s over 5e7 characters) is not_checked. Its statuses are verbatim, near_verbatim (similarity at least 0.90, or 0.95 under 40 characters, five words or more), unverified and not_checked. At the default settings it decides nothing: verified and match are the existing check’s, as before, and only accept_near_verbatim (below) lets its status stop the iterative reader. On a labelled set of 343 true and 162 false quotations it rejects 1.2% of true ones (95% CI 0.3% to 3.0%) against 36.4% (31.3% to 41.8%) for the existing check, and accepts none of the 52 with a changed digit, 8 with a changed number word, 3 with a changed comparison sign, 37 with a flipped negation or 16 invented sentences; it does accept 25 of 46 quotations with one content word swapped as near_verbatim, which is why that status is not verified. Rscript dev/quote-matcher-rates.R prints the full table.

Parameter schemas, declared calls and reader costs

  • New hr_schema(), hr_param() and hr_validate() state a spec’s parameters once: type, default, range and choices. gr_read_spec(), gr_segment_spec() and gr_ingest_spec() now check their arguments through schemas instead of code of their own. They accept the same values and return the same specs, with the same clamps, defaults and warnings; a clamp warning now also has class hr_param_clamped beside gr_clamped.

  • A value outside the choices of context_order, restate, on_overflow, context_source, ocr or layout is still an error, which now names the setting and has class gr_bad_setting, where it used to be a plain match.arg() error that said 'arg'.

  • Readers and segmenters declare the labels their calls carry. gr_register_reader() and gr_register_segmenter() take a new calls argument, the stems of their calls’ trace labels ("stuff.answer", c("map.answer", "reduce")). gr_readers() and gr_segmenters() list them in a new calls column. A reader or segmenter registered without calls declares its own name, which covers labels such as "longest.answer" for a reader called "longest".

  • A reader states its cost as a function. gr_register_reader() takes a new cost argument, a function of (input_stats, params) returning the new hr_cost(): requests expected and at worst, embedding requests, and what the reader must send. The pre-flight check of gr_read() adds up these functions instead of repeating each built-in reader’s call pattern, and the governor decides from the sum whether the run fits its limits before the first request. The built-in readers’ estimates, the trace’s preflight step and the refusals are unchanged. A registered reader without cost is counted as before, one request per chunk. cost_calls is kept for display only, as the description gr_readers() shows; the pre-flight check never reads it, and it may be retired in a later release. A cost function may also return a plain list with calls_max and no calls, which is read as both. hr_cost() has a tokens_out_max for a reader whose replies can be billed beyond the reply cap; the check prices every request at input_stats$out_cap, the largest cap the run’s model is sent, and uses tokens_out_max when it is larger.

  • hr_param() with a type or tier it does not know is an error of class gr_bad_setting that names the parameter. A named_map parameter takes a character vector or a list whose elements are all named.

Pipeline options

Each new setting below is off by default, so a default run sends the requests it sent before, keeps its store, cache and replay keys, and returns the tables it returned. Each is declared with its evidence (untested unless a source is named), is listed by gr_settings_table(), and has a walkthrough that says how to test it with hr_sweep().

  • gr_extract() gains resolve = "vote", which keeps the value most of a document’s chunks gave, for no extra request; a tie goes to the earliest of the tied values, as "first" chooses. agreement_columns = TRUE adds <field>_agreement (how many of the chunks that reported a field give its most common value, as "2/3") and <field>_conflict to the table. An abstract that says 240 and two results paragraphs that say 236 give 240 under "first", 236 under "vote", and "2/3" with a conflict under both. Each answer’s notes$agreement holds the same counts.

  • gr_screen() gains criteria_schema. At "per_criterion" each reply also gives every criterion’s status, "met", "not_met" or "not_reported", which the table holds in criteria_status, and an exclusion needs an inclusion criterion "not_met" or an exclusion criterion "met": a reply that excludes with a criterion not reported and none not met is recorded as "unclear", for a person. The default, "decision", sends the request and schema it sent before.

  • gr_screen() gains samples and sample_rule. Above 1 sample, each document’s screening request is sent that many times as separate draws (each with its own draw_index, so a cache keeps them apart), and "include_if_any" includes a document any draw included, excludes one only when every draw excluded it, and leaves the rest "unclear"; "majority" takes the decision most draws gave. The table gains sample_decisions and include_share. At the default, 1, one request is sent as before.

  • gr_segment_spec() gains packing and runt_merge. packing = "balanced" keeps the number of chunks greedy packing makes and evens their sizes (paragraph, sentence, recursive, structural, semantic). runt_merge = "both" merges a first chunk under min_tokens forward into the second, which the backward merge could not reach. The defaults, "greedy" and "backward", pack as before.

  • gr_segment_spec() gains semantic_threshold. At "texttiling", the semantic segmenter cuts by TextTiling’s depth score (Hearst 1997): the similarity between the windows before and after each gap, read from the same embeddings, cut at valleys deeper than Hearst’s cutoff and than the spread of the similarities, so a text on one topic gets at most about one cut instead of one gap in ten. The default, "percentile", cuts as before.

  • gr_segment_spec() gains table_packing. At "grouped", paragraph packs each table on its own and opens every chunk of it with the table’s header row, so a 60-row table cut into three chunks gives three chunks that each start with the header. The default, "rows", packs rows as before.

  • gr_ingest_spec() gains ocr_trigger. At "after_running_lines", under ocr = "auto", a PDF page is counted against ocr_min_chars once the running heads, feet and stamps the layout pass drops are taken out, so a scanned page whose text layer holds only a 60-character fax header or Bates stamp is OCR-ed. The default, "raw_text", counts the whole text layer as before.

  • gr_ingest_spec() gains ocr_confidence. At TRUE, the blocks of a PDF page OCR read carry ocr_confidence, Tesseract’s mean word confidence for the page, from a second Tesseract pass over each OCR-ed page. The default, FALSE, runs one pass, as before, and adds no column.

  • contextual with context_source = "llm" now sends each chunk’s section path from the document’s headings ("Methods > Participants") with its request, and declares its cost, one request per chunk and no more, in $extra$cost and a segment.cost trace step. proposition keeps the page and section of each batch on its chunks, and counts propositions with no support in their batch (a number it does not give in any form, “1,200” for “1200” or “twelve” for “12”, or most words absent) in $extra$propositions_unsupported. The new setting proposition_check = "drop" drops them, counting them in $extra$propositions_dropped with a gr_proposition_dropped warning; the default, "count", keeps every proposition as before. The new setting proposition_context_tokens sends each batch that many tokens from the end of the batch before it, as context; at its default, 0, each batch is sent alone as before. The section path changes what contextual sends under "llm", an opt-in setting of an opt-in segmenter, so its cache and replay keys change; no default segmenter sends anything new.

Screening

  • Kappa is no longer reported alone. Each agreement table carries Cohen’s kappa, PABAK and Gwet’s AC1 with intervals, the prevalence and bias indices, and the class-wise sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV; $agreement$kept$paradox flags a table whose prevalence index is above 0.8 in absolute value, where kappa says more about prevalence than agreement. $decisions holds the 3x2 counts, and print() and the audit report show them with the agreement set. The rate of "unclear" decisions is the existing "deferred to a person" metric, with its interval.

  • The kappa interval is a bootstrap over documents. It is a percentile bootstrap with B = 2000 under a fixed seed, so the same sample gives the same interval and the session’s random stream is untouched; B and the seed are in $agreement$kept$bootstrap. AC1 keeps Gwet’s (2008) variance. Where the screener and the person agree on every record, disagree on every record, or the sample holds fewer than 10 records, the kappa and AC1 intervals are left empty (NA) with a $note saying why, instead of a zero-width interval such as [1.00, 1.00].

  • print() on a calibration now shows the 3x2 counts on every sample, including one drawn from a single stratum. The audit report’s calibration section shows the same counts, and sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV with intervals beside kappa, PABAK and AC1.

  • Unclear records no longer leave a review without a word. A gr_screening gains $forward (the included and unclear records, the set a review reads at full text) and $deferred (the unclear ones). gr_extract(screening) still reads only $included in this release and now warns (class gr_unclear_dropped) when that leaves unclear records out; from 0.9.0 it reads $forward. Pass screening$forward to read them now. Passing the vector screening$included gives no such warning: $included stays a plain character vector in this release, and a warning on that path is left to a later release.

  • New gr_resolve() records a person’s decision on a deferred or failed record: who decided, when (in UTC) and why, in the table and as a "screen.resolve" step in the trace. forward, deferred and included are rebuilt, the screener’s own decision is kept in screener_decision, and gr_calibrate() compares against that one, so a person’s correction is not credited to the screener. Duplicates of a resolved record take the same decision. The audit report’s screening table shows the screener’s decision and who resolved each record, when and why.

  • gr_flow() accounts for every screened record. A record with no decision is now counted as “could not be read” only when no screening call was made; one whose call failed, or whose reply was not the form asked for, has a row of its own, “screening call failed”. New rows count the records resolved by a person, the records kept for full text ($forward) and, of those, the ones deferred ($deferred).

  • New gr_search_recall(records, known, tier, held_out) measures a search against a seed set of papers already known to be relevant: the share it found, with a Clopper-Pearson interval from hr_prop_ci(), overall and for each tier. Seeds are matched to records by the rules gr_records() uses to find duplicates. A seed those rules refuse (a title under 12 letters or digits, a title and year shared by records with different DOIs, or authors or venues that disagree) counts as not found and is listed in $refused with the reason. Seeds used to build the search, marked by a used_to_build column or left out of held_out, are left out of the figure and listed in $excluded. When known is a gr_records() that holds two exports of one paper, the copy its duplicate_of marks is counted once with the seed it copies and listed in $copies. An empty seed set, a tier with no seed or none left, and a tier string that names no column of known (with one seed too) are refused. The help cites relative recall (Sampson et al. 2006) and PRISMA-S.

  • gr_audit_report() gains recall, its last argument, which adds the search’s recall against the seed set and the seeds it missed. Calls that pass arguments by position keep their meaning.

  • gr_read_many(), and so gr_screen() and gr_extract(), check that each file is the paper its record names when the sources come from a gr_records(): the first 6,000 characters of its text are searched for the record’s DOI, as a whole DOI, and title, with any HTML markup such as <i> taken out of the record’s title. When the recipe’s cleaning removes digits (remove_numbers, in the "legacy" preset), the DOI is not looked for and the title is compared without its digits. A last identity column of $summary holds TRUE, FALSE or NA (nothing to check), and FALSE warns with class gr_identity_mismatch and is added to warnings. Nothing is dropped and gr_flow() is unchanged. print() counts the mismatches, and the audit report lists them. A row restored from store keeps its check only when the run that stored it checked the file against the same record; otherwise identity is NA, the stored warning is dropped, and a note in warnings says the check needs the document read again. A run without records has no new column, even for rows it restores from a store a run over records wrote, and those rows lose the stored warning.

  • Screening recall now says what it is relative to. print() on a gr_calibrate() result and the audit report state that recall is the share of the records the person judged eligible that the screener kept, wherever they report recall or sensitivity. The audit report now gives recall with its interval and one-sided bound as well.

  • gr_calibrate() gains $worst_case, a sensitivity analysis that counts every record the reviewers split on as eligible and works out recall, records lost and the verdict again. With several reviewers, print() and the audit report show it beside the main estimate. With one decision per document it repeats the main figures.

  • The audit report’s header gives, for each stage, when it ran and the harnessr version that ran it, from the stage’s own trace, beside the time and version that wrote the report. A stage run on another version is flagged. “What this report does not establish” now says what each check looks at: the quote check, the value check behind n_unverified, and for a write-up the citation and figures checks.

Screening recall against a target

  • gr_reference(of = "stacked") draws the reference the screening help recommends in one sheet: every record the screener kept, and n of those it excluded. Each row records its stratum and its inclusion probability (1 for a kept record, n / N for an excluded one). A blind sheet keeps both inside a key per row of one length, so they do not reveal what the model decided. frame = is accepted as another name for of. The other frames draw exactly as before.

  • gr_calibrate() estimates recall on a stacked reference instead of refusing it: the ratio of Horvitz-Thompson totals, K / (K + M), with M the projected number of eligible records excluded and exact hypergeometric bounds on M mapped into a one-sided lower bound on recall. A kept sheet and an excluded sheet stacked with rbind() are read the same way with of = "stacked"; without it they are still refused.

  • gr_calibrate() gains recall_target (0.95), conf (0.95) and max_lost, and its result gains recall, lost, false_exclusion, work_saved, unclear_rate, strata and verdict, which says whether the one-sided lower bound on recall reaches the target (or the bound on M is within max_lost). A sample of everything screened bounds recall with Clopper-Pearson, except that when it is every screened record recall is known exactly and is its own bound (method = "census": 25 of 25 eligible kept gives a bound of 1, not the 0.887 Clopper-Pearson gives); a sample of the exclusions alone bounds M but not recall. The fields it returned before keep their meaning, apart from kappa (see “Other changes to requests and results at the default settings”).

  • New gr_screen_sample_size() gives the reference size a recall target needs: n >= ln(alpha) / ln(T) eligible records with no miss (59 for 95% at 95% confidence), divided by prevalence for the records to draw, and for a sample of the exclusions the exact hypergeometric size for a frame of frame_n records with at most max_lost lost, beside the binomial one. For a sample of everything screened, giving frame_n with prevalence caps the draw at the frame: a frame of 500 records at 5% prevalence holds about 25 eligible records, fewer than the 59 needed, so n is 500 (judge every record) rather than 1180. A smaller draw cannot pass gr_calibrate(), which bounds such a sample with Clopper-Pearson: 388 records with 22 eligible and none missed give a bound of 0.873.

References from several reviewers

  • gr_reference(reviewers = k) writes one decision column per reviewer, human_decision_1 to human_decision_<k>, and a consensus column for an adjudicator, one row per document. With one reviewer the sheet is as before.

  • New gr_reference_consensus() forms one decision per document from several reviewers, by rule = "majority" (a tie is settled by consensus where filled, and otherwise settled as include), "any_include" or "adjudicated" (the consensus column, an error where reviewers disagree and it is empty). It also reads a long sheet with a reviewer column. Each row says in consensus_from how its decision was reached. Columns named human_decision_<x> are reviewers, except those ending in _note, _notes, _comment, _comments or _date.

  • gr_calibrate() compares the screener with the reviewers’ consensus on a multi-reviewer sheet, and stops only on a disagreement nobody settled, saying how many there were. Its result gains reviewers: agreement between each pair of reviewers from hr_agreement() (kappa beside PABAK, AC1 and the prevalence and bias indices, never alone), Krippendorff’s alpha with three reviewers or more, and each reviewer’s sensitivity and specificity against the consensus. On a stacked reference both are weighted by the stratum weights recall uses, with exact hypergeometric bounds for the rates and a bootstrap within the sampled stratum for agreement; the notes flag the weighted kappa interval as approximate when fewer than 100 excluded records were sampled. A one-reviewer calibration is unchanged.

Claims and the write-up

  • gr_claims() gains unverified, last. At its default, "exclude", a value whose quote did not verify, or that came with no quote, is left out of the claims prompt, so no claim rests on it, and a study with no value left is not sent. "include" shows them, marked unverified with the quote that was given. The result gains $values, every value with its status ("verified", "unverified" or "not reported") and quote, and $unverified, the unverified values listed apart; print() counts them. The default is untested.

  • gr_synthesise() shows the unverified values to the writer, marked, and gains $values and $sentences: every sentence of the text as published, linked to the studies it cites that are verified records (with at least one value whose quote verified), or flagged as citing no study or no verified record. print() counts the flagged sentences, and the audit report lists them and the values the claims prompt left out. Nothing is marked partial for a flag.

  • The figures check of gr_synthesise() links each figure found in a row to the field it reports, in a new field column of $figures ("n (study 2)"), and gives pool, how many distinct values the rows it was checked against hold, and chance, the chance of a match among them by coincidence, from the digits the figure was written with. A sentence that cites nothing is still checked against every row its section was shown, but a figure found there now counts only when its chance is below 0.05 or the sentence names the field it matched for that figure (a one-letter field just before it, a longer name in the same clause): an uncited “63%” among 40 numbers is unbacked, “n = 236” matching a field n of 236 is backed, and in “(n = 410), 57 dropped out” the 57 is not backed by n. A qualified figure (“about 50”) counts as near a row’s value only in a sentence that cites the row. The check stays diagnostic only: it marks nothing partial and sends nothing. The audit report adds pool and chance to its unbacked figures.

  • gr_synthesise() gains $uncited, the studies the text as published cites nowhere, from the final cited set the reference list follows, with shown, whether any section’s prompt held the study. print() gives one line and the audit report a table. It is a count, not a quota: nothing asks that every study be cited. The result also keeps $section_studies (the studies each section was shown), $closing, $style, $figure_bands and $bib_columns.

  • New gr_recheck(synthesis, text_marked) checks and renders an edited write-up again. Edit $text_marked, the marker form, and pass it back: a marker naming a row that does not exist, or a study the section under whose heading it stands was not shown, is left as a marker, counted in $recheck and warned about (gr_recheck_citations); the citations and reference list are rendered from the edit; and $figures (stage "edited"), $sentences, $uncited and $contradictions are worked out again, the figures with the style and figure_bands the write-up was made with. A study one heading cites without being shown it keeps its reference when another heading cites it honestly. On a synthesis saved before $section_studies was kept, shown in $uncited is NA. Nothing is sent.

  • gr_synthesise() gains $contradictions: with claims, sentences that state a claim and cite a study on its contradicting side with no hedge (“may”, “suggest”) and no word of contrast (“however”, “mixed”). A sentence states a claim when it stands in a section the claim was given, points in the claim’s direction in one of its clauses (so “improved mood, with no adverse events” still states that mood improved) and shares at least two content words with it. It is found by counting words, with no model; print() counts them and the audit report lists them. Nothing is marked partial.

  • gr_claims() and gr_outline() record their calls the way the other review stages do. Each records on a trace of its own and, given trace =, adds its calls to that trace when it finishes, as gr_screen(), gr_extract(), gr_read_many() and gr_synthesise() already did. Before, both recorded straight onto the trace they were given, so a review trace that an earlier stage had taken past hr_options(max_calls =) or max_cost_usd = stopped them before they sent a request, and gr_claims() returned no claims, marked partial. Pass one trace to every stage and its totals are the sum of the stages’, with each request counted once.

  • gr_outline() no longer adds to claims$trace. Given no trace, it recorded its calls on the trace of the claims it was handed, which changed a finished gr_claims() result and made claims$trace report the outline’s cost as the claims’. Its calls are now on attr(outline, "trace"), which gr_outline_pick() keeps and gr_synthesise() keeps as $outline_trace. Scripts that totalled a review’s cost from claims$trace after gr_outline() should pass one trace to both, or add attr(outline, "trace"). The audit report’s claims row still includes the outline’s calls, read from the synthesis, and counts them once when a script passes trace = claims$trace to gr_outline().

Comparing recipes

  • gr_compare() says what each recipe cost. summary gains calls, tokens_in, tokens_out and usd, priced from the requests on the trace at each model’s registered price, and usd_estimated, the share of those dollars spent on requests whose token counts were estimated locally because the provider reported none (NA for a trace whose requests do not record how their counts were obtained, such as one saved by an earlier version). A recipe is charged for a segmentation it shares with an earlier recipe, as it would be run alone, so the column can add up to more than hr_trace_cost(cmp$trace). usd is NA when a model has no registered price. The columns come after error and before premise.

  • gr_compare(correct =) takes strings that a right answer contains (ignoring case and white space) or a function of each gr_answer returning TRUE, FALSE or NA, and adds correct and usd_per_correct, the cost of a right answer: usd when the answer is right, Inf when it is wrong and cost something. Without it the summary has no such columns. A recipe a limit stopped before it found anything is NA, not wrong: the spending, token or call limit, the model allow-list, the output ceiling, or a spending limit refusing a model with no price. A correct function that fails or returns something other than one logical gives a gr_bad_correct warning and NA for that recipe, so the paid results still come back; an invalid correct argument is an error of the same class.

  • gr_compare()’s help now says it is descriptive, and points to hr_benchmark() and hr_report() for a comparison with intervals.

Sweeping settings

  • hr_sweep() builds one arm per row of a grid of settings. The base is an arm from gr_arm(), whose settings each row overrides by name, a chain from hr_chain(), swept by path (see “Steps and chains”), or a function of the grid’s columns that returns an arm. A column that is not a setting is an error (class hr_unknown_setting) listing the settings that are, and rows that build the same configuration are dropped with a message (class hr_sweep_collapsed).
  • hr_benchmark() adds a param.<name> column for each setting the arms record (arms from gr_arm() or hr_sweep()), after reportable, so a sweep is summarised with aggregate(correct ~ param.top_k, bench, mean). It warns (class hr_same_config) when two arms resolve to the same configuration: two recipe arms whose settings resolve to the same recipe, or two other arms that differ only in name.
  • hr_sweep_check() lists the arms of a benchmark that sent byte-identical requests to an earlier arm on every item and run, and the recorded settings that differ between them. Those settings changed nothing that was sent: top_k under the fast recipe, which sends the whole document, is one.
  • gr_settings_table() returns every setting of every stage in one table of 228 rows: the ingest, segment and read schemas (with the entries of cleaner_opts and layout_opts the built-in code reads), the arguments of the screening, extraction, synthesis and evaluation functions, and every hr_options() option. Each row has its stage, the function that takes it, its default, tier, evidence status and source, the first sentence of its help, and the guide section that explains how to choose it. It is built from the schemas, the option rules, the functions’ arguments and the installed help when it is called, and a test fails when a declared setting is missing from it.
  • gr_settings() returns the schema of the read, segment or ingest settings, and as.data.frame() of a schema gives each setting’s default, range, tier, evidence status and source.

Settings that were constants

Values that were fixed in the code are now settings, each with the value it had as its default, so a run at the defaults sends the same requests and keeps the same cache, store and replay keys. A new read, segment or ingest setting is stored in the spec only when it is not its default, and a new option is recorded in a trace’s options, and joins a key, only then. Each setting’s help says where its default came from; almost none has a measurement behind it.

  • hr_options(): auto_max_tokens (50000) and auto_room_share (0.5) set when answer_document(recipe = "auto") reads with "fast"; reasoning_floor (2048) is the least output cap sent to a reasoning model, and 0 turns the raise off; output_reserve_share (0.25) is the share of the window hr_budget() reserves for the reply; near_verbatim_sim (0.90), near_verbatim_sim_short (0.95) and near_verbatim_short_chars (40) set when the edit-distance matcher scores a quotation near_verbatim. A non-default reasoning_floor joins the response-cache key, and it, output_reserve_share and the near-verbatim settings join the store key of gr_read_many().
  • gr_read_spec(): accept_near_verbatim (FALSE) lets a near-verbatim quotation stop the iterative reader under verify = TRUE, and is refused without it; max_merge_levels (6) caps the merge tree of map_reduce and the other merging readers, and the worst case counted before a run counts that many levels; restate_tokens (1200) is the length above which restate = "auto" repeats the question; bm25_k1 (1.5) and bm25_b (0.75) are the BM25 parameters of rerank’s prefilter and lexical retrieve, the usual values in Robertson and Zaragoza (2009); lexical_blend (0.5) weighs cosine against BM25 in an offline retrieve.
  • gr_segment_spec(): context_reply_tokens (90) and context_document_tokens (1500) for contextual under context_source = "llm", and proposition_reply_tokens (2000) for proposition.
  • gr_ingest_spec(): layout_opts changes the PDF running-head pass (depth, share, min_pages, max_chars, max_words). Under cleaner_opts, references_after (0.4) sets where the references cleaner may find a bibliography heading; it keeps the code’s behaviour, a heading at or after 40% of the text, which a comment had described as “the last 40%”. header_max_chars and header_min_repeats, which headers_footers already read, are now documented. The settings column of gr_compare() names each entry of layout_opts and cleaner_opts, as layout_opts.depth=3, and the ingest step of a run’s trace records them under settings when any is set.
  • gr_synthesise(): coherence_rounds (1) lets each revision pass run more than once, each round checked as a pass is and the pass stopping at a round that is discarded or changes nothing (paper-orchestra runs up to 3, with no recorded evidence for that number); figure_bands (about 0.10, over and under 0.25) sets how near a qualified figure must be; prominence (thirds) sets how many claims get each sentence budget; and study_weights takes a function that weighs the studies claims are ranked by. $coherence has a round column.
  • gr_calibrate(max_width = 0.10), hr_report(auto_bootstrap_at = c(items = 300, clusters = 30), min_runs = 5) and hr_calibrate_signal(min_errors = 100, isotonic_min_items = 1000, min_clusters = 20). None of these numbers was measured. The coverage simulation (dev/sim-coverage.R) measured the two interval methods at two designs only, 386 items in 40 clusters and 50 items in 10; the switch to the bootstrap at 300 items and 30 clusters lies between them and is itself untested. A calibration record held to a bar other than the default says so in its notes.
  • hr_param(evidence =) must be a list of status ("measured", "cited" or "untested") and a non-empty source. Every parameter of the read, segment and ingest schemas declares one, their help pages list them under “Where the defaults come from”, and print() of a schema shows each parameter’s tier and evidence status. Each schema keeps at most five basic parameters: the read spec’s are reader, model, top_k, cite and verify, and the rest are advanced. No default changed.

Evaluation: benchmarks, judges and statistics

Agreement and estimation statistics

  • New hr_prop_ci() gives Wilson, Clopper-Pearson or Jeffreys intervals for proportions, vectorised over x and n, two-sided or as a one-sided bound. Wilson matches prop.test(correct = FALSE), including a lower bound of exactly 0 at x = 0 and an upper bound of exactly 1 at x = n (the formula alone left a rounding error there for 38 and 60 of the values of n from 1 to 200, such as a lower bound of 2.8e-17 at 0 of 10), and Clopper-Pearson matches binom.test(). The help says which to use: Wilson for descriptive rates, Clopper-Pearson for any “at least” or “at most” guarantee.

  • New hr_agreement() reports agreement between two raters as the count table with observed agreement, Cohen’s kappa (standard error and a bootstrap interval over items), the prevalence and bias indices, PABAK, Gwet’s AC1 with its variance interval, positive and negative specific agreement, and, when positive is given, sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV against the second rater. paradox_flag marks tables where kappa should not be compared across samples. For a matrix of coders, or a level other than nominal, it reports Krippendorff’s alpha at the nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio level with a bootstrap interval, and reports only percent agreement, with a note, below 30 items or for a constant field. It has print() and as_json() methods, and its bootstrap leaves the caller’s random state as it was. Factor levels that neither rater used are left out of the two-rater table with a note, and a positive label that is not among the labels is an error. When coders’ factors carry different level sets, ordinal alpha merges them keeping each coder’s order (low, high and low, mid, high give low, mid, high), and levels that conflict or leave two levels unordered are an error.

  • New hr_ht_estimate() estimates a total (Horvitz-Thompson), a mean (Hajek) or a ratio of totals from a sample drawn with known inclusion probabilities, optionally stratified, with the difference estimator when predictions for the whole population are given, and a bootstrap interval that resamples within strata with the finite population correction (the Rao-Wu rescaling bootstrap). A stratum judged in full (pi = 1) adds no variance: a census of 20 records gives se 0 and the interval [12, 12] for a total of 12, and a simple random sample of 100 from 200 with 30 eligible gives se 6.5, the design value.

  • New hr_ppi() gives a prediction-powered estimate of a mean from many model-labelled units and a few labelled by people, with the power-tuned PPI++ weight by default and inverse-probability weighting when the labelled units were drawn with unequal probabilities.

  • New hr_alt_test() runs the alternative annotator test of Calderon, Reichart and Dror (2025): whether a model’s labels can be used in place of three or more human annotators, with the margin set by their declared expertise, a Benjamini-Yekutieli correction, the winning rate, and the winning rate over margins from 0.05 to 0.20. Annotator column names must be unique and non-empty.

Agreement on extracted fields

  • New gr_extract_agreement() compares two extraction tables for the same documents, a model’s gr_extract() result against a person’s or two people’s, matched on document. Each field gets Krippendorff’s alpha at a declared level (levels =; by default interval for integer and number fields and nominal otherwise) with a bootstrap interval over documents, percent agreement and the number of documents compared. “Not reported” is a category of its own in a nominal field; an ordinal, interval or ratio field gets a separate row for agreement on whether it is reported, and its value row covers the documents both tables report. Below 30 documents or for a constant field alpha is NA and a note says why. Rows of a gr_extract() result that failed or were read only in part are not taken as reporting nothing, duplicates are left out (a blank duplicate_of, as a table saved with write.csv(na = "") reads back, is not a duplicate), and $pairs lists every cell side by side for reading the disagreements.

Benchmarks: arms, references, scorers and hr_benchmark()

  • New hr_arm() describes one configuration to compare: a function of an item and a context that carries the client, a trace of the run alone, the governor and the run’s draw_index, with ctx$call() as a shortcut for hr_call() that fills in all three. run is required. The arm records its settings, a version and a hash of its code and settings, which is the same in every session and after saveRDS(), also for an arm built inside a function of yours. The hash covers the values the code reads from where it was written, the workspace included, so an arm at top level that reads a global prompt gets a new hash when the prompt changes.

  • New hr_reference() holds the items to score, their labels, clusters, splits ("dev", "exploratory", "calibration", "test", "final"), inclusion probabilities, strata and coder labels, with a content hash. Labels, clusters, splits, inclusion probabilities and strata given with names are matched to the items by name (c(q2 = "Lima", q1 = "Paris") gives q1 Paris), and names that are not the item ids are an error of class hr_bad_reference. Items can be added with hr_reference_add() until a benchmark starts scoring the reference; after that every copy of it, and every reference grown from it, refuses new items with an error of class hr_reference_locked.

  • New hr_scorer() states the scoring contract (correct, outcome and failure kind for each run), and hr_scorer_exact(), the default, compares text after folding case and white space, and sorts parse failures, errors, NOT_IN_DOCUMENT and failures an arm reports itself apart from wrong answers. A number in a label is compared in plain digits, so the label 100000 accepts "100000".

  • New hr_benchmark() runs every arm on every item of the chosen splits runs times (5 by default; fewer warns) and returns one row per cluster x item x arm x run with correctness, failure kind, tokens by kind, cost and its provenance, seconds, the draw index and the id of the run’s trace. Run r is draw r, so repeated runs are separate cache entries and recorded draws, and an arm whose runs come back as one stored reply (the same cache entry, a repeated replay, a repeated response id) is refused with an error of class hr_duplicate_draw. Each draw is also recorded under the arm’s name, and hr_replay_client() answers an arm only with its own replies, so replaying some of the arms, or the arms in another order, gives each arm what it got even when two arms sent the same request. Stages called inside an arm with trace = ctx$trace, such as gr_read(), gr_segment() or answer_document(), send their requests at the run’s draw too; a request given a fixed draw_index still sends that one. The whole benchmark is held to one governor; a run with a refused request is recorded as a budget stop and counted wrong, and so is a run that a reader’s pre-flight check stops with gr_call_cap or gr_cost_cap, in an arm from gr_arm() or one of your own. The benchmark warns (class hr_budget_stopped) with the number of runs stopped, the limits that stopped them, how many count against an arm, and the first run stopped.
