With no governor the limits are hr_options()’s, set for one run of a reader (400 calls), and the warning gives the values of the options that stopped runs and, for a call, spending or token limit, says to pass a governor sized for the benchmark. A reader stopped by its own check before its first request leaves a budget.preflight note on the run’s trace naming the limit, and the errors that check raises carry the limit in $limit. Every run on an item with no label has correct = NA, failures included, so such an item never counts against an arm. Rows on the dev split are marked not reportable. print() shows accuracy per arm over the reportable rows and labelled items, with the dev split’s accuracy in its own column, descriptive only.

  • The ctx an arm’s run receives has three more shortcuts, each sent through the run’s client, trace, governor and draw. ctx$call_json(messages, schema, ...) makes a structured call and returns the parsed reply, or a failed gr_result when the request failed or the reply does not meet the schema, which the scorers count as an error. ctx$judge(candidates, ...) calls hr_judge() with trace = ctx$trace, so the judge’s cost is in the run’s usd once; pass rubric as hr_judge() needs. ctx$note(name, value, refs = NULL) records a signal about the run’s item with hr_signal().

  • hr_signals() accepts an hr_bench. It reads each run’s own trace and adds arm, run and item columns; the benchmark’s folded trace is not read, so each signal is listed once.

  • Self-judging is recorded. hr_scorer_judge() takes judge_model, the configuration’s model by default, and hr_benchmark() adds a self_judged column: TRUE when the judge’s model equals the model or served model of one of the run’s requests, FALSE when the run asked a known model and none equals it, NA otherwise. The match is exact and nothing is refused; hr_report() adds a note counting the self-judged runs per arm. hr_bench has the new column before reportable.

  • New hr_error_correlation() says how far a benchmark’s arms fail on the same items: the phi coefficient between each pair’s errors within strata of item difficulty (or strata you give), pooled over the strata; the share of items both got wrong where they gave the same wrong answer (Kim et al. 2025); and a sample of items every arm got wrong, for a person to check. It reads the benchmark’s rows and sends nothing. Yen’s Q3 from a one-parameter mixed model is not computed, since it would need lme4, which harnessr does not depend on.

Benchmark reports: hr_report()

  • New hr_report() turns the reportable rows of an hr_benchmark() into accuracy per arm (mean over runs within each item, then over items) with intervals that keep clusters together. With the default method = "auto" and at least 300 items and 30 clusters it uses method = "bootstrap", a studentised (bootstrap-t) cluster bootstrap: it resamples whole clusters with all their items, runs and arms (B = 2000, or 5000 with confirmatory = TRUE), each resample studentised by its own linearised standard error. Below either threshold it uses the new method = "cluster_t", a cluster-robust t interval on the logit scale: the linearised variance of the ratio estimator with the C / (C - 1) factor and t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom (Cameron and Miller 2015). Both can be asked for at any size. Where neither is defined (accuracy 0 or 1, or the same in every cluster) the arm gets Korn and Graubard’s interval, one-sided from the bound at 0 or 1, with a note. method = "exact" gives Clopper-Pearson on the effective number of items from cluster totals (Korn and Graubard) instead, with items rather than runs as trials, and method = "bayes" a Bayesian beta-binomial model with a cluster random effect and flat priors, with a note on its calibration. No interval treats items or runs as independent trials.

    The coverage simulation (dev/sim-coverage.R, 2000 replicates) chose these methods over a BCa cluster bootstrap and the Bayesian model, which failed it: BCa covered 93.5% for accuracy at 0.75 and 92.9% for the paired difference with 40 clusters, and 89.2% for the difference with 10 clusters; the Bayesian model covered 96.5% to 96.6% with 10 clusters, its misses 2.9% to 3.2% below the truth and 0.2% to 0.5% above. With the methods above the same simulation passes: accuracy 95.5% and 95.0%, difference 94.7% with 40 clusters; accuracy 95.8% and 95.7%, difference 95.7% with 10 clusters.

  • The report also gives paired differences between arms (every pair, or the ones in contrasts) with cluster-robust t intervals on C - 1 degrees of freedom at every size, cut to [-1, 1] (when every cluster gives the same mean difference, so the cluster variance is 0, Tango’s score interval with the items as pairs and the item count scaled for C - 1 degrees of freedom, with a note), single-step max-t simultaneous intervals over all pairs from the multivariate t with the same correlation (Hothorn, Bretz and Westfall 2008), and bootstrap rank intervals in place of a ranking by point estimate. A pair whose cluster variance is 0 takes Tango’s interval at the Bonferroni share (1 - conf) / number of pairs, and the max-t critical value over the rest is then taken at 1 - (1 - conf) x (pairs with variance above 0) / (number of pairs), so the family stays at conf: with 3 pairs, one at variance 0, and 12 clusters it is 2.43, where the full-level 2.20 left the family at up to 6.7% error. The critical column is NA on the Tango rows. print() shows the simultaneous interval of a contrast written against benchmark order (b - a) as the negated interval of its pair, [-upper, -lower]. The report also gives flip rate, TARa and run-level SD; pass^k with the unbiased estimator; dollars and tokens per item and per correct item with intervals, flagging arms whose cost rests on estimated token counts for more than 5%; the cost-accuracy frontier with each arm’s share of resamples on it; failure counts with accuracy recomputed without parse failures and refusals; and within-item and between-item variance on the probability scale, with a note to use 10 runs when runs account for more than 10%. Below 5 runs the report is descriptive only, without intervals. An item scored on some runs but not all is refused. It has print() and as_json() methods and leaves the caller’s random state as it was. The BCa intervals used for cost and pass^k count a resample as below t0 only when it is more than 1e-12 x max(1, |t0|) below it, so a resample that ties with t0 up to a rounding error is not counted. This is the count in exact arithmetic; boot.ci() counts sum(t < t0) and can differ when there are such ties (484 against 495 of 999 resamples in one test, moving the limits by less than 0.001).

Non-inferiority contrasts and the minimum detectable difference

  • New hr_mdd() and hr_n_needed() give the smallest paired accuracy difference a clustered design can detect, and the items needed for a given one, from n_eff = (t_(C - 1, 1 - alpha’) + t_(C - 1, power))^2 x p_disc / Delta^2 with t quantiles on C - 1 degrees of freedom for C clusters, the degrees of freedom of the report’s non-inferiority bound, and the design effect DE = 1 + (m - 1) x ICC_D, where ICC_D is the intra-cluster correlation of the paired item difference and m becomes (cv^2 + 1) x m for unequal clusters. With n_contrasts above 1, alpha’ is alpha / n_contrasts, the first step of Holm. For 480 questions in 80 documents at ICC_D 0.2 and p_disc 0.2 this gives DE 2, 240 effective items and an MDD of 8.2 points, or 10.7 points after Holm over nine contrasts (8.1 and 10.4 with normal quantiles). hr_n_needed() finds the number of items by root finding, since the degrees of freedom depend on it, and both refuse a design of one cluster. hr_n_needed() also takes a true difference below 0. Its print() rounds the clusters up first and gives the items as that many clusters of m: 840 items in 140 clusters of 6 for n_items 837.8.

  • New hr_contrast() and hr_register_contrasts() fix non-inferiority contrasts (arm, reference arm, margin, whether it must also be cheaper) against an hr_reference() before a benchmark scores it. A confirmatory margin below the design MDD at 80% power after Holm is refused with an error of class hr_margin_below_mdd; with confirmatory = FALSE it is registered as exploratory. The check is at one-sided alpha 0.025 or less whatever level the design was given at, and a design with more items or clusters than the reference holds on the test and final splits is refused. A reference already being scored, or one rebuilt with the same content, is refused (hr_registration_after_scoring), and the registration is hashed. hr_mdd() takes whole numbers of items and clusters only.

  • hr_report() gains registration. Each registered contrast is non-inferior only if the one-sided lower bound of the accuracy difference is above -margin and, when it tests cost, the upper bound of the paired cost difference (BCa cluster bootstrap) is below 0. The accuracy bound is the cluster-robust t bound of the report’s paired differences, taken one-sided on C - 1 degrees of freedom (the Tango bound with items as pairs when every cluster gives the same mean difference), so at one-sided 0.025 it is the lower end of the printed 95% contrast interval. A BCa cluster bootstrap bound undercovered the paired difference in the coverage simulation (92.9% with 40 clusters, 89.2% with 10). Confirmatory contrasts are tested with Holm’s step-down procedure, exploratory ones at alpha. The design and achieved MDD are printed beside every verdict (the achieved one on the linearised standard error and the same t quantiles as hr_mdd(), and NA when the cluster variance is 0), and a contrast that passed its registered test is reported as passed even when the achieved MDD exceeds its margin. Tango’s (1998) paired score interval on effective counts, at most one pair per item, is given as a cross-check. A changed registration, or one for another reference, is refused. Each contrast’s p_value is the smallest one-sided level at which it passes, found by bisection down to 1e-6. With a cost test the search stops at 1 / (B + 1) (1 / 2001, about 5.0e-4, at B = 2000): below that level the BCa cost bound is the most extreme resample and stops moving.

  • Dev-split rows are refused as evidence. A report with a registration or confirmatory = TRUE errors with class hr_dev_not_evidence when the benchmark holds rows on the dev, exploratory or calibration split or rows marked not reportable.

Benchmarking reading recipes

  • New gr_arm() and gr_arms() wrap reading recipes as benchmark arms. Each run reads the item’s document with answer_document(), or with gr_read() when the document is already chunked, and returns the gr_answer, with every request on the run’s own trace. That trace gives every request of the run, segmenter and reader requests included, the run’s draw index, so repeated runs under a cache or a recording are separate draws. A reader that refuses to start because the run’s call or spending limit leaves too little returns a partial NOT_IN_DOCUMENT answer noting the limit, which is scored as a budget stop rather than an error. The arm records the recipe and its settings, and its version is the package version.

  • New gr_qa_reference() builds an hr_reference() of questions about documents from questions, documents and acceptable answers (one string or a list of alternatives per question). Unanswerable questions, given as flags, ids, positions or the answer NOT_IN_DOCUMENT, are labelled NOT_IN_DOCUMENT. The payload an arm is given holds the question and the document only: whether an item is unanswerable is in its label. Items are clustered by document by default.

  • New gr_scorer_answer() marks an answer right when it contains an accepted answer after folding case, white space and thousands separators ("1,204" matches "1204"), with numbers matched whole ("12" is not in ".12" or "-12", but is in "12-15", and "45.2" is in "45.2m"), a numeric label written in plain digits, and an unanswerable item right when is_not_found() is true and no limit or refusal stopped the run. Wrong answers are sorted into parse failures, budget stops, refusals, not_in_document and wrong.

Judges and their validation record

  • New hr_judge() asks a model to choose between candidates ("select"), compare two ("pairwise") or grade one against a reference ("grade"). Candidates are shown under the letters A, B, … only, and each item is asked in two presentation orders: reversed for candidates, reference first and then response first for grading. A verdict that differs between the orders, mapped back to the candidate it names, is returned as "unresolved" with degradation = "judge_inconsistent"; a failed request or a reply with no allowed verdict is "failed". One order is allowed for grading only. With more than two candidates, orders above 2 shows cyclic rotations. Requests go through the same path as hr_call(), so the governor, a cache keyed with draw_index and the trace all apply, under the labels judge.<mode>.o<k>. Given a trace, the judge is a step of the run that trace records: its requests count against the trace’s governor, go out at the trace’s draw index and draw scope unless draw_index names another, and are folded into the trace when the judgement ends, each naming the judge in its judge field. The note it adds records no tokens, so cost summaries count the judge once. A governor given with a trace is applied with the trace’s, the lower of each limit, so a judge inside a benchmark run cannot take the run past the benchmark’s max_calls. self_judged in hr_benchmark() leaves the judge’s requests out. $trace and $judge_cost hold the judge’s requests alone. A judge called without a trace, and hr_scorer_judge(), keep their calls apart.

  • New hr_judge_config() holds what decides a judge’s answers (model, mode, rubric, the package’s instructions for the mode, reply schema, orders, how verdicts are combined, the positive grade) with a SHA-256 hash of them.

  • New hr_judge_validate() and hr_judge_valid(). From blind human labels on a judge’s decisions, the record gives Cohen’s kappa with a bootstrap interval and the full hr_agreement() set, sensitivity and specificity with Wilson intervals (and the sensitivity half-width), and the swap-inconsistency rate. Items the judge left unresolved or failed on count as not called positive, the rule hr_scorer_judge() applies, so the figures describe the judge as the scorer uses it. Fewer than 50 human-positive or 50 human-negative items are refused with hr_judge_too_few_labels, and the minimums cannot be lowered. Text labels such as "pass" and "fail" default to the configuration’s positive grade. A judge column that shares no value with human (logical calls beside "pass"/"fail" labels) is refused with gr_bad_setting rather than counted as all negative. The optional columns consistent, outcome and config_hash are read by exact name, so an extra column such as consistently_long is ignored. The record is keyed by the configuration hash; hr_judge_valid() is FALSE, naming what changed, when the model, rubric, prompt, schema, orders, aggregation or positive grade differ, or when the record was edited.

  • New hr_scorer_judge(), a benchmark scorer that grades each output against its label with a grade-mode judge. It refuses to be built without a valid record (hr_judge_unvalidated). Unresolved judgements count as wrong and failed ones as errors, and the judge’s requests stay in the scorer’s own trace, out of the benchmark’s cost columns. A draw_index argument sets the cache draw for the judge’s requests.

  • New hr_judge_ppi() corrects judge-scored accuracy with human labels on a sample through hr_ppi(): prediction-powered inference, and the inverse-probability weighted DSL form when the labelling probabilities vary. It also reports the uncorrected judge mean. Its normal interval needs enough labelled items in every inclusion stratum; with few labels at small inclusion probabilities it is too narrow.

Baselines without a model

  • New hr_tfidf() turns texts into an l2-normalised tf-idf matrix: lower-cased runs of letters and digits, terms in at least min_df texts (at most max_features, the most frequent), raw counts times the smoothed idf log((1 + n) / (1 + df)) + 1. It is a dense base R matrix, which suits a reference or screening set of a few thousand texts.

  • New hr_baseline_classifier(), a ridge-penalised logistic regression on tf-idf features fitted by iteratively reweighted least squares and cross-fitted by fold, so each item is predicted by a model that never saw it. Folds are stratified by label, or keep each cluster whole. The vocabulary and idf are fitted on each training fold only. More than two labels are fitted one against the rest. It returns the out-of-fold probabilities and labels, the training size of each fold, and accuracy with a Wilson interval from hr_prop_ci().

  • New hr_baseline_ranker() simulates prioritised screening over a fully labelled set, as ASReview does: it starts from seed_n relevant and irrelevant records, refits after each batch, and screens the record with the highest predicted relevance next. The model is the same ridge logistic regression or multinomial naive Bayes. It returns the screening order, the recall curve, the records screened to reach 95% recall, WSS@95 and the number a random order would need on average.

  • New gr_stop_test(), the hypergeometric stopping test of Callaghan and Muller-Hansen (2020) for prioritised screening. After each screened record it gives the p-value for recall still being below target given the records left unscreened, and the first point where screening may stop at alpha. It takes a vector of relevance in screening order, with unscreened records as trailing NA, or an hr_baseline_ranker() result.

Drift checks

  • New hr_drift_check() reruns an arm live on the items of a frozen hr_benchmark() and reports, item by item, which items were lost, gained or moved, with their most common output before and after. Two tests are fixed in the call, with alpha and an optional alert threshold. (a) The accuracy change, live minus frozen, by a BCa cluster bootstrap over documents on paired item accuracy, with the clustered McNemar test of Obuchowski (1998) beside it as a cross-check. (b) Excess instability: the flips between frozen and live runs against the flips among replicate runs, frozen and live, one-sided, on the same cluster resamples. Per item it estimates the squared change in accuracy, so it sees losses and gains that cancel in accuracy and noisy items that turn deterministic; it needs at least 2 live runs. The alert is crossed when the whole accuracy interval lies beyond the threshold, and alert_not_ruled_out reports the weaker reading, an interval that reaches beyond it. Moved items whose runs disagreed are counted apart in the printout, since their moves can be run-to-run variation. Fewer than 5 frozen runs is refused (hr_drift_few_runs), as are a changed arm, another reference or scorer (hr_drift_mismatch) and a live rerun answered from a cache or a recording (hr_drift_not_live). The live rerun is returned as an hr_bench.

Validation of the intervals and the MDD

  • A nightly validation job checks the report’s statistics on simulated benchmarks. dev/sim-coverage.R simulates clustered corpora with a known effect, document ICC and run variance, reports each with hr_report(), and gives the coverage of the accuracy and paired difference intervals over 2000 replicates with its Wilson 95% interval, in a large design (386 items in 40 clusters, studentised cluster bootstrap) and a small one (50 items in 10 clusters, cluster-robust t on the logit scale, with the Korn-Graubard interval beside it). An interval passes when that Monte Carlo interval contains 95% and its lower end is at least 93%. dev/sim-power.R sets hr_mdd() against a power simulation of the report’s cluster-robust t non-inferiority bound and passes when the simulated MDD is within 1 point. Both exit with status 1 on a failure. The workflow .github/workflows/validation.yaml runs them every night and by hand, never on pull requests, and keeps the printed tables as an artifact. The power table’s power_check column also marks a design whose simulated power at the formula’s MDD lies below or above the target beyond Monte Carlo error (“below target” or “above target”), without failing the run.

  • The hr_mdd() help gives the power simulation’s result (2000 replicates, seed 1): the MDD was 0.16 and 0.17 points below the simulated one at 80 equal clusters (simulated power at the formula’s MDD 78.55% and 78.30%) and 0.25 points above it at 40 unequal clusters (81.60%). With normal quantiles it was 0.26 and 0.41 points below at 80 clusters (power 77.20% and 76.05%, short of 80% beyond Monte Carlo error), which is why the formula takes t quantiles.

Signals, calibration records and gate thresholds

  • New hr_signal() and hr_signals(). hr_signal() records a value the package produced about its own work (a self-signal) into a trace, as a local step labelled "signal"; it sends no request, so requests and cache keys are unchanged. hr_signals() reads every recorded signal back from a trace, an answer or a list of them as one table, a row per value, with the value as text and as a number. A trace object reached twice in the list is read once; two separate traces are both read even when they share a run_id (two traces made with hr_trace(run_id = "pilot") give 2 rows, not 1).

  • Three readers record a signal. iterative records gr.iterative.can_answer for each step whose reply parsed, preview records gr.preview.skip for each section of a usable plan (the plan’s own decision, before any section is demoted to skim), and ensemble records gr.ensemble.adjudicate as "model", "concatenated" or "single member". No reader behaves differently: each answer, each request and each cache key is as before, and a trace from these readers has one more local step per signal.

  • New hr_calibrate_signal() measures a signal against a graded set that must include unanswerable items, on the half of each cluster’s items not used to fit the map: the Brier score with its reliability, resolution and uncertainty decomposition (and the two within-bin terms that make it exact over binned forecasts), type-2 AUROC, the area under the risk-coverage curve with the selective risk at 50, 80 and 90 percent coverage, and the debiased equal-mass calibration error over 5 to 10 bins, each with a cluster bootstrap interval (NA when the calibration half has one cluster, with a note below 20 clusters). AUROC and the risk-coverage curve are taken on the signal itself, so a signal that is higher when the item is wrong shows an AUROC below 0.5 even after the map turns it round. The map is Platt scaling, isotonic regression (only from 1000 graded items, counted before the split) or none. A map that does not increase with the signal keeps the record advisory. The record is keyed by served model, model version, task, format, prompt hash, effort, module and contract version, starts advisory, says why, and has print() and as_json() methods.

    The ECE and the Brier decomposition use the same bins, and items with the same p always share one, so the ECE does not depend on row order. bins is the number of bins formed: 2 for a logical signal, which therefore stays advisory under the 5-bin rule. A graded set with a split column is calibrated on its calibration rows alone, with the rows left out counted in notes and a message, and one with no calibration row stops with hr_bad_calibration. Columns are read by exact name, so a cluster_size column is not taken for cluster.

  • New hr_calibration_valid() is FALSE when any key field of a record differs from the run’s, and names the fields.

  • New hr_gate_threshold() picks a threshold by Learn-then-Test: the thresholds are tested from strict to loose with a one-sided Clopper-Pearson bound on the error among accepted items, or on the miss rate for exclusions, and the loosest one before the first failure is kept. The bound is taken on an effective sample, n / deff items with k / deff errors, where the design effect deff is the cluster variance of the error rate over the variance with each item its own cluster, never below 1. Items from one document are not independent: with 30 documents of 20 items, a true error rate of 0.12 and an intraclass correlation of 0.3, a gate at alpha = 0.10 and delta = 0.05 that took the items at face value passed in 8.7 percent of draws, and with the design effect it passes in 2.4 percent. Unclustered items give deff = 1 and the exact Clopper-Pearson bound. $gate reports deff and n_eff, and $gate$path the deff of every threshold. It starts where enough items are acted on for the bound to reach alpha, and reports "none passed" or "too few items" when nothing qualifies. A record becomes "gating" only with a passing threshold, at least 100 wrong items in the graded set, a map that increases with the signal and an ECE over at least 5 bins.

  • New hr_signal_policy() and hr_apply_signal(). A signal gates its action only with a gating record for the same signal and action whose key matches the run; otherwise it stays advisory (gated = FALSE), the item is routed to a check, a person or nowhere, and reason says why. Nothing in the package calls hr_apply_signal() yet, so nothing gates by default.

Splits and label sheets

  • New hr_assign_splits() assigns reference items to the dev, exploratory, calibration, test and final splits by cluster, so every item of a document lands in the same split. The default shares are 10% dev, 10% exploratory, 30% calibration and 50% test. Each cluster’s place comes from the SHA-256 digest of the seed and its id, so the assignment does not depend on row order or the session’s random state. With method = "stable" (the default) adding or dropping documents never moves another one; method = "balanced" gives each split its share of clusters by largest remainders. The result reports clusters and items per split beside the target shares, and warns with hr_empty_split when a split given a share receives nothing. A whole-number cluster id is hashed written in full, so document 300000 gets the same split stored as a double or as an integer. Columns are matched by exact name: a frame with no item_id, id or cluster column does not take ideal_answer for its ids or cluster_size for its clusters.

  • New gr_label_sheet() writes a CSV for people to label, with an instructions file beside it, for five kinds of set: QA answers, a screening reference, extraction fields, a calibration graded set and judge validation verdicts. Each row has an item_id and empty decision columns. A blind sheet (the default) copies only the columns a person needs to judge the item, so no model output or sampling detail reaches it. With several reviewers each gets a sheet of their own. The help page gives the number of items each set needs for the package’s own evaluation. Ids come from a column named exactly item_id or id; a frame with neither gets qa-0001, qa-0002 and so on, so a column such as ideal_answer never reaches the item_id column of a blind sheet.

  • New gr_read_labels() reads filled sheets back, checks every value and id, and stops with gr_bad_labels naming the sheet, row and item of each value it cannot read. It returns a screening reference that gr_calibrate() and gr_reference_consensus() take, an extraction table for gr_extract_agreement(), and calibration labels with clusters, with the items’ own columns joined back by id (an item column named like a decision, such as the model’s answer or a judge’s verdict, comes back as model_<name>). Only a calibration sheet written with blind = FALSE has the correct column hr_calibrate_signal() needs; a blind one gives reference answers, and the model’s answers are scored against them to make correct. A blind = FALSE calibration sheet read back without items turns its model_score column back into the number score, so it is a graded set either way. A blind screening sheet carries the reference’s frame as an opaque key, so it reads back as a usable reference without items.

  • gr_label_sheet("pairwise") writes two texts per row as text_1 and text_2, in an order drawn for each row from a SHA-256 digest of its id and texts, with the order kept in an opaque order_key tied to the row. gr_read_labels() gives the person’s choice back in candidate order as "A", "B" or "tie", ready for hr_judge_validate(positive = "A"), where a tie counts as negative. A key edited or moved to another row is an error of class gr_bad_labels.

Segmentation metrics

  • New gr_seg_pk() and gr_seg_windowdiff() measure how far a segmentation’s boundaries fall from a reference’s (Beeferman, Berger and Lafferty 1999; Pevzner and Hearst 2002), with NLTK’s windows and default k, so values match NLTK’s on the same strings. gr_seg_boundaries() turns chunks, or a reference segmentation given as text, into the sentence-by-sentence boundaries they compare. It locates segments and sentences in the document, so a sentence the document repeats, such as “See note 3.” at the start of two sections, stays in the section it occurs in. gr_seg_recall() ranks each segmentation’s chunks for each question as the retrieve reader does and reports recall at k per segmenter, with no model call under the lexical embedder.

Steps and chains

Steps and chains are opt-in and add no setting, so a default run sends the requests it sent before, with the same cache keys. vignette("compose") shows them at work.

  • hr_step(name, fn) builds a step: a function of (input, ctx) with the settings it was built with recorded beside it. With a schema, its settings are checked and resolved by hr_validate(); with build, the function is built from the settings when the step is, so a bad setting fails there. input and output declare what the step takes and returns.
  • hr_chain(..., name) runs steps in order as one hr_arm(), which hr_benchmark() takes as it takes any arm, and hr_sweep() sweeps by path (see hr_set() below). Inside a chain each step gets ctx$step and ctx$step_params, and ctx$params is the arm’s. hr_chain(old, judge = NULL, name = "nojudge") derives a chain without one step; x = step replaces a step and a new name adds one. The arm records each step’s settings as "step.setting", and its configuration is a hash of the steps’ code, the values it reads and their resolved settings. A step that takes chunks no earlier step returns warns (hr_chain_gap), and a step that cannot follow an answer is an error (hr_bad_chain). A step that takes a document no earlier step returns does not warn, since most chains start at the segment step, which ingests at the default settings.
  • hr_settings(x) lists every setting of a step or a chain: one row per setting of each step’s schema, with the step, the setting, its resolved value, whether it was given, and the schema’s default, range, type, tier and evidence. A chain’s settings are named by path, "step.setting". An arm from gr_arm() or hr_arm() is an error (hr_bad_arm) that points to gr_settings_table().
  • hr_set(x, ...) builds a step or a chain again with some settings changed: hr_set(chain, retrieve.top_k = 8), or hr_set(step, top_k = 8) for a single step. A path that is not a setting of a step’s schema, including a fixed extra setting, is an error (hr_unknown_setting). The values are checked as when the step was built, so an out-of-range number is clamped with a warning, each changed step keeps its class, and the chain’s configuration is that of the new settings: a setting set to its default gives the configuration of leaving it out. hr_sweep() uses it to sweep a chain by path, as in hr_sweep(chain, data.frame(retrieve.top_k = c(2, 8))), which gives param.retrieve.top_k columns in the benchmark.
  • New gr_step() builds one stage of a run ("ingest", "segment" or "read") as an hr_step (class c("gr_step", "hr_step", "function")), with its settings checked against the ingest, segment or read schema when the step is built and its input and output declared, and gr_step_retrieve() returns the chunks retrieve would send, ranked and scored, without the answer request. Inside an hr_arm() run function or an hr_chain() they use the run’s ctx$client and ctx$trace, so a benchmark counts and limits their requests.

Command steps

hr_step_command() is opt-in: no command runs unless you build a step with one, so every default run sends the requests it sent before, with the same cache keys. Its three settings are declared with their evidence (untested), are listed by gr_settings_table() under the evaluate stage, and have walkthroughs in vignette("evaluate") that test each with hr_sweep().

  • hr_step_command(name, argv, parse, timeout, held, wd) builds a chain step that runs a program you name, through system2(), and reads its result as "passed", "failed", "error" or "timeout". Each element of argv is one argument, quoted for the shell and never split; there is no default command, and argv is never taken from a model’s reply. argv may be a function of (input, ctx), for a command that names a file an earlier step wrote. OPENAI_API_KEY is unset for the call and put back after it; the rest of the environment is inherited. parse = "testthat" reads the last testthat summary line, and gives "error" when there is none. A program stopped at timeout seconds carries the degradation "command_timeout". The run is noted in the trace as "step.command", with hashes of the command and the output, never the output.
  • With held = FALSE the step adds its result to its input as $check. With held = TRUE it passes its input on, records the signal "command.<step>" and attaches the result as attr(output, "hr_held"), for a scorer. hr_chain() refuses a step that is not held after one that is, with class hr_held_not_last.
  • hr_judge() reads its "judge_inconsistent" degradation from the same list of codes as the command step. Nothing it returns changes.
  • vignette("compose") builds a coding sub-agent: a draft step, a visible check, a revise step that reads it, and a held check last that only the scorer sees, compared with the first draft alone. It also runs the two goals the steps were written for, a recipe swept over a grid next to an arm of your own and a chain with a judge step derived and swept, and says why a stand-in model’s handler must be stateless. A test builds the same loop from exported names only, on four small tasks, and checks it with hr_check_module().

Skills

Skills are opt-in: a step has one only when you give it hr_skill(), so every default run sends the requests it sent before, with the same cache keys. A skill adds no setting to gr_settings_table(): its limits are fixed, and whether a skill helps is tested by comparing a chain with and without it, as the “Skills” section of vignette("compose") does with hr_benchmark(), hr_report() and an hr_sweep() over a function.

  • hr_skill(path) reads a skill folder you choose: SKILL.md, whose header (name, description, version, between two --- lines) is read without a YAML parser, and whose body is the instructions; text files under references/; and scripts under scripts/, which are listed and never run. A nested or multi-line header value, a missing name or closing line, a nul byte, a file linked from outside the folder, more than 50 files in either subfolder or more than 200,000 bytes in all is an error of class hr_bad_skill; an unknown header key warns (hr_skill_unknown_key). Its hash covers the header, the instructions, the references and every byte of the scripts. The package never looks for skills and never lets a model choose one, and a skill’s text goes into the prompt as it is, so it can carry prompt injection.
  • hr_step(skill = ) takes a skill. Inside hr_chain() the step’s ctx$call() and ctx$call_json() send the instructions and references as a system message before the step’s messages, and ctx$skill holds the skill. The hash is a fixed setting of the step and part of its fingerprint, so a chain with a skill has its own configuration and records the setting "<step>.skill" (a param.<step>.skill column in a benchmark). The skill’s version, when it has one, is the step’s version. gr_step() and gr_step_retrieve() refuse a skill with class hr_bad_skill, since their requests are not sent through ctx$call().

Registering modules and the module contract

Nothing here changes a default or adds a setting, and no request or cache key changes: each gr_register_*() function keeps its arguments and checks, and the built-in cleaners and extractors keep their registration stamps, so ingest cache keys do not change. Each gr_*() listing keeps its columns and adds version and contract at the end, so code that picks a column by name, or by its position counted from the first column, reads what it read before. The module contract is version 0.2, and CONTRACT.md lists its fields. The “Registering any kind with hr_register()” section of vignette("extending") shows the new functions.

  • hr_register(kind, name, fn, ..., description = "", calls = NULL, version = NULL) registers a module of any kind through that kind’s own function, so it runs the same checks: hr_register("reader", ...) refuses what gr_register_reader() refuses. The kinds are "extractor", "cleaner", "segmenter", "reader", "embedder", "protocol" and "step"; any other is an error of class hr_unknown_kind, and calls for a kind that declares no calls is an error of class gr_bad_setting. A module you register with hr_register() records the version you give and contract 0.2 in its entry. An entry registered with a gr_register_*() function has neither field, and each listing shows NA for it.
  • hr_register("protocol", name, fn = protocol) registers a protocol from gr_protocol() through gr_register_protocol(). hr_register("step", name, fn) registers a step from hr_step(), or builds one from a function of (input, ctx) and the arguments you pass. It refuses call stems that are blank or contain whitespace, with class gr_bad_setting, and keeps each stem once, as the reader and segmenter kinds do. The package registers no step at load. Parallel workers receive the steps you registered, so hr_modules("step") on a worker lists them.
  • hr_modules(kind = NULL) lists the modules of every kind in one table: kind, name, description and calls, a list column of the call stems each module declares, then version and contract. With kind, it adds that kind’s own columns, such as a reader’s signature or an extractor’s extensions.
  • gr_readers(), gr_segmenters(), gr_cleaners(), gr_extractors(), gr_embedders() and gr_protocols() end with the columns version and contract. The built-in segmenters register through hr_register(), so they show contract 0.2.
  • hr_register("segmenter", ...) also takes effort_label, a function of the segment spec that returns the label the segmenter’s requests carry. The built-in segmenters register this way, so a run’s effort map reaches each one as the effort for its own label, as before. A function you register under a built-in’s name with gr_register_segmenter() still gets the whole map.
  • Reads that look up a module by name, such as running a reader, choosing a segmenter’s effort or picking an embedder, go through the kind’s accessor, and hr_embed() looks embedders up the same way. The core calls no document layer function.
  • When an embeddings request fails, hr_embed() falls back on the embedder registered as "lexical", so if you replace "lexical" with gr_register_embedder() your function also serves as the fallback. If your function fails there, hr_embed() warns with its error and uses the built-in hashed lexical vectors.
  • Signal calibrations have a contract version of their own, 0.1, apart from the module contract, so a calibration record stays valid under hr_calibration_valid() when the module contract moves.

Conformance checks

Nothing here changes a default or adds a setting. hr_mock_client() without mode keeps the fields and replies it had, and no request or cache key changes. “Checking a module against the contract” in vignette("extending") shows a mode in use.

  • hr_mock_client() gains mode, which breaks each chat reply the way a provider can: "bad_json" sends a JSON object cut off part way, "refuse" sends an empty reply that hr_call() reports as failed, "at_cap" marks the handler’s reply as cut off at the output cap and bills the cap (a failed result from the handler comes back as it is), and a vector of HTTP status codes such as c(429, 500, 200) gives call i the i-th status, marked retryable for the statuses the HTTP transport retries. Embeddings are left as they are. Pass such a client to gr_check_reader() or gr_check_segmenter() to check a module against replies that fail.

  • The package’s own tests check every registered module that hr_modules() lists, and every protocol, against the rules for its kind. An extractor is checked where its packages are installed and the tests have a sample file in its format. Extractors are checked for blocks with text and typed columns, cleaners for one string per block, some text left and the same result twice, embedders for finite unit-length rows under their own name, and protocols for a question, criteria, an outline and a save and read that gives the same protocol back. Every built-in reader and segmenter passes its rules under each mock mode, and every reader keeps to a call cap of 0, 1 and 3. These checks are internal.

  • New gr_check_reader() and gr_check_segmenter() run one registered reader or segmenter on gr_example() through an offline mock client and report which rules of its contract it breaks. A reader is checked for finishing without an error, returning a gr_answer with the fields gr_read() documents and a single string as its answer, evidence and chunks_used that name only chunks of the input, call labels covered by the stems it declared in calls, and no more requests than its cost function’s worst case for that input. A segmenter is checked for finishing without an error, returning a gr_chunks with the documented columns, text in every chunk, unique chunk ids, no chunk over max_tokens that gr_segment() had to split, and call labels covered by its declared stems. Every built-in reader and segmenter passes them.

  • New hr_check_module() is the core helper both use: it runs a closure that calls a module in a temporary working directory, catches its error and warnings, asks a named list of rule functions about what came back, and returns an hr_conformance data frame with a rule, ok and detail for each. ok is NA for a rule that could not be checked. print() lists the broken rules first, says “passes all N rules” when every rule passes, and says “passes all N rules checked; M not checked” when some rules could not be checked.

  • The checks are reports only. gr_register_reader() and gr_register_segmenter() still check only that fn is a function, and register a module that breaks a rule as before.

Changes and fixes

  • BM25 scoring is faster on many chunks. Document frequency is counted once per query term instead of once per term for every chunk, so the rerank prefilter and the offline retrieve path no longer slow down with the square of the number of chunks. Scores are unchanged.

  • print() of a gr_calibration no longer shows “NA” for the frame size. A reference given as a plain data frame does not record how large its frame was, and the example in ?gr_calibrate printed sampled from: all (NA of 8 screened). For of = "all" the frame is every screened record, so gr_calibrate() now fills $frame$frame_n with the screened count and the line reads all (8 of 8 screened). For any other frame with no recorded size it reads excluded (8 screened; frame size not recorded). Estimates, intervals and the exclusions projection do not change.

  • gr_calibrate() counts $frame$screened_n from the records the screener decided when the reference does not record it, the count gr_reference() writes. It used every row of the screening table, so a plain data frame from a run with undecided rows printed all (58 of 60 screened) where the same rows from gr_reference() printed all (58 of 58 screened).

  • A worker in a parallel batch sets OPENAI_API_KEY for each item and puts back the value it had when the item ends. A key passed as key or through the harnessr.api_key option no longer stays in the worker process after its item. A worker started from a session with OPENAI_API_KEY set has that key from the start and keeps it. A backend handler or hr_ellmer_client() that reads the key from the environment still gets it. A batch through hr_mock_client() sets no key. Requests and cache keys do not change.

  • A gr_claims, gr_synthesis or gr_calibration you saved with an earlier version gets the fields added since filled with their defaults when gr_gaps(), gr_outline(), gr_synthesise(), gr_recheck() or gr_audit_report() reads it, or print() reads a gr_claims or gr_synthesis. Each one gives the output it gave for that object before. gr_recheck() returns the filled object, and gr_synthesise() stores the filled claims table in $claims. A hand-built object such as structure(list(table = tab), class = "gr_screening") passes through unchanged. Requests and cache keys do not change.

  • A download refused for size no longer breaks the downloads after it. httr shares one curl handle per host, and a stream stopped at the size limit could leave that handle attached to its connection, so every later download from the same host in the session failed with “Handle is already in use elsewhere”. Each request now gets its own handle.

  • Every block of a document says which table it is a row of, if any: gr_ingest() adds table_id and table_rows to $blocks (each unbroken run of "table" blocks is one table; table_rows is "3" for a row from Word or HTML, "1-12" for a Markdown table read as one block), and paragraph chunks of a document with a table carry table_id and table_rows for the rows they hold. This is provenance only: no text and no request changes, and a document with no table gets no new chunk columns.

  • An embedded image in a Word file whose OCR fails now raises a gr_ocr_failed warning naming the image, as a PDF page does; before, its text was lost with nothing said.

  • semantic run on lexical vectors now reports its method as "semantic->lexical", as it reports "semantic->paragraph" when it falls back. This is a label fix: the chunks and the requests are unchanged.

Documentation

  • New guide, vignette("core") (“The core: calls, clients and results”), in a new Core group on the site and in the README. It covers calls made with no document: hr_call() with each kind of client, every field of a result, the trace and how to read it, structured replies, a check that runs a program on a reply, signals, and the classes of the core’s errors and warnings. Its settings walkthroughs cover model, api, api_base, api_headers, embedding_model, max_retries, retry_pause_base, request_timeout, temperature and actor, and gr_settings_table() links those options to them.
  • New guide, vignette("models") (“Models, prices and tokens”), in the Core group. It covers what the registry knows about a model and how sure it is (hr_models(), hr_model_info(), hr_model_limits()), adding a model and setting prices (hr_register_model(), hr_load_models()), cost estimates (hr_estimate_cost()), models with no price and old prices, and token counting (hr_count_tokens(), hr_tokenizer(), hr_set_tokenizer()). Its settings walkthroughs cover unknown_model_action, allow_unpriced, price_max_age_days and tokenizer, and gr_settings_table() links those options to them.
  • New guide, vignette("context") (“Context: budgets, fitting and cutting”), in the Core group. It covers how much room a prompt has (hr_budget() and its guarantees), fitting named pieces into it (hr_context_fit(), hr_context_policy()), cutting one piece with each keep rule (hr_truncate(), hr_truncate_tokens()), and the cuts the trace records, with one overflowing report under five policies. It says that harnessr does not summarise a conversation, and shows a summary built as a step. Its settings walkthroughs cover safety_margin, output_reserve_share and min_output_tokens, and gr_settings_table() links those options to them.
  • ?hr_budget gives the default reply reserve as output_reserve_share of the usable window rather than a fixed quarter, and says that a reserve leaving no input room, an explicit one included, drops to min_output_tokens before the error. ?hr_options says that output_reserve_share does not change how much of a document a reader fits, since the readers give max_answer_tokens as the reserve.
  • New guide, vignette("effort") (“Effort: how hard the model reasons”), in the Core group. It covers which models take a reasoning effort and what a model that does not reason is sent, the levels, the request field and a client’s extra_body default, an effort per call label, what reasoning costs, what effort does to the response cache, a replay and the trace, effort raised for the next stage (hr_effort_escalate(), hr_effort_event(), hr_effort_log()), and hr_effort_check() on a benchmark of fixed and raised efforts. Its settings walkthrough covers reasoning_floor, and gr_settings_table() links that option to it.
  • The site and the README group the guides in two parts after Get started. Core holds core, models, context, effort, runs, compose, evaluate, compare and settings; Documents holds ingest, segment, readers, review and extending. The reference index lists the core functions first, by topic in the order of the core guides, then the document layer.
  • The README and vignette("harnessr") introduce harnessr as a harness for model calls with a document layer built on it. The get started guide shows a call, its trace, prices and limits, context and effort before the first question about a document.
  • The README is a short front page, and each topic has a guide of its own. Beside the guides described here, vignette("segment") (“Cutting documents into chunks”), vignette("review") (“Many documents and literature reviews”), vignette("runs") (“Limits, caching and replay”), vignette("compose") (“Composing steps into chains”), vignette("extending") (“Extending harnessr”) and vignette("migrate") (“Upgrading from older versions”) are new. vignette("harnessr") replaces vignette("readgpt") as Get started, and vignette("tour") is gone: each of its topics is in one of the guides.
  • Each document guide (ingest, segment, readers, review, extending) opens by naming the core pieces it builds on, and links to the core section where it mentions a budget, the trace, a refusal, the cache, effort or a price. vignette("compose") and vignette("evaluate") open as core guides. vignette("settings") lists the core settings before the document settings.
  • ?gr_result lists every field a result carries, including cached, served_model, response_id, fingerprint, attempts and, for a request the limits did not send, refused and refusal.
  • ?hr_cache no longer says that every structured reply that does not parse is kept out of the cache. That holds for the package’s own structured calls; hr_call() does not parse a reply, so it caches one like any other.
  • New guide, vignette("compare") (“Comparing methods and settings”), works through five comparisons offline, each ending in an hr_report(): three readers on 32 test questions in 8 reports, a grid of three segmenters at two chunk sizes, top_k swept over 1, 2 and 4, two values of screen_tokens, and a pairwise judge validated against 180 labelled pairs. Settings are tuned on the dev split and one chosen contrast is run on test, with 10 runs where the report’s notes ask for them and simultaneous intervals where three arms are compared. A last section shows the same steps on your own documents, writing results to a directory you name.
  • A settings reference. vignette("settings") prints every setting of every stage from gr_settings_table() when it is built, each important one linked to its walkthrough, and the extractors, cleaners and presets, segmenters, readers, embedders and recipes from their registries. vignette("harnessr") gains a “What you can change” section: one row per stage with its count of settings, the most used, and links to the walkthroughs; Get started also gives the basic settings of each stage with when to change each.
  • Settings walkthroughs. Nine guides end with a “Choosing the settings” section, one walkthrough per important setting or group: what it controls and trades off, the signs in your results that point to changing it, where its default came from (measured, cited or untested), and how to test it with hr_sweep(). Besides the core guides above, vignette("ingest") covers cleaning presets with references_after, and OCR; vignette("segment") the segmenter, chunk size, overlap, packing, semantic boundaries, tables, and contextual and proposition; vignette("readers") the reader, top_k, mmr, word matching, placement, verify with cite, outcomes, premise checks, effort, merges, context_policy with refine_state, and the preview and rerank safeguards; vignette("review") screening calibration and replies, extraction and synthesis; vignette("runs") the global limits and the governor. The offline examples run on the stand-in models and report what each value sent: on the example report, "scan" cleaning sent the same requests as "standard", a merge cap of 6 the same as a cap of 1, mmr = 0.7 the same as plain top-k, and verify the same as no check.
  • New guide, vignette("evaluate") (“Measuring and comparing configurations”), covers reference sets and label sheets, benchmarks and their reports, non-inferiority, judges, baselines, drift and signals; vignette("review") gains recall against a target, the stopping test, several reviewers and agreement on extracted fields.

Version 0.6.0 (readgpt)

New

  • Reasoning effort, set stage by stage. The default models reason before they answer, and that reasoning is billed as output and counted inside the reply’s cap. Nothing in a read, a corpus run or a write-up said how much of it to do, so every call went out at the provider’s default: the hundreds of per-chunk extraction calls of a corpus reasoned as long as the one call that drew its claims. The only lever was a client’s extra_body, which set one effort for every request and was invisible to recipes, store keys, comparisons and traces.

    effort sets it. One string applies to every call. A character vector named by call label sets it per stage, such as c(extract = "low", "synthesise.section" = "high"): a name covers a label equal to it or starting with it and a dot, the longest matching name wins, and an unnamed or "default" element covers the rest. It is a gr_read_spec() setting, so it reaches gr_read(), answer_document(), gr_read_many(), gr_screen(), gr_extract() and the segmenters that call a model. gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_synthesise() take it as a new argument at the end, and gr_call() takes it after .... The help for gr_read_spec() lists every label and suggests a profile: low for the many mechanical stages, high for the few that judge.

    It is sent as reasoning = {effort} on the Responses API and as reasoning_effort on Chat Completions (replacing an effort a client’s own reasoning object carries), and only to a model the registry lists as a reasoning model, since others refuse the field. A mock or backend handler sees it as params$effort. An ellmer chat cannot take it per call, so it is not sent there, and a warning says so once (gr_effort_unsupported); its trace steps keep the effort asked for as params$unsent_effort, so the trace and gr_audit_report() do not count it as sent. Unset, nothing changes: no body field, no handler parameter, no key part, so every cache, recording and corpus store made before still answers. Set, it is part of the response-cache key, the corpus store key, what gr_compare() counts as a different recipe (recipes whose segmenter is sent the same effort still share their chunks), and the key a replay matches on; a replay under another effort misses and says it was recorded at a different one, and one under the same effort matches even in a session that has not registered the recording’s model as a reasoning model. Each request’s effort is on its trace step and in an effort column of as.data.frame(trace), and gr_audit_report() shows it beside what each stage cost.

  • A question the document contradicts gets a correction, not an answer. Asked “Why did revenue fall in 2023?” of a report in which revenue rose, a reader either answered on the question’s terms, offering a cause for a fall that did not happen, or replied NOT_IN_DOCUMENT because the report gives no reason for a fall. Either way the one thing the document does say about the question was lost, and the second reported silence where the document contradicted the question.

    gr_read_spec(premise = TRUE) adds a third outcome. The prompts that answer the question tell the model that when the excerpts state the contrary of an assumption in it, it is to say so in one sentence giving what they state instead. That sentence is $answer and $premise, and is_not_found() is FALSE for it. Excerpts that are merely silent are still NOT_IN_DOCUMENT. map_reduce drops a chunk that lacked the answer, as before, but passes a chunk that contradicts the question to its merge as a finding, and the merge may report the premise false itself; notes$premise_chunks keeps which chunks said so whatever it decides. Every answering reader handles the outcome, iterative through its schema. gr_compare() and gr_read_many() gain a premise column, and print() and the audit report say the model reported it, because the verdict is the model’s reading of the excerpts and nothing checks it against the document. It is off by default because it changes what is sent: a run without it sends exactly what it sent before, so caches, recorded replays and corpus stores still answer it. Screening and extraction ignore it.

  • The figures in a review are checked against the rows they cite. gr_synthesise() checked that every [study N] pointed at a row the section was given, and nothing checked what the sentence said that row found. “d = 0.61 [study 3]” over a row reporting 0.41, or “1,240 participants” over a row of 1,204, was a clean, fully cited sentence. A revision pass could also change 0.41 to 0.61 after the fact with every guard passing it, because the markers, the hedges and the claims were all where they had been.

    Every number in every sentence is now looked for in what the writer was shown for that sentence: the rows it cites as the prompt showed them, the question and the brief, and with claims the claims resting on those rows. This runs on the draft and again on a kept revision that changed it. A figure found nowhere is listed in $figures, counted in $sections$n_unbacked, shown by print() and the audit report, and warned about (gr_synth_unbacked_figures). It does not mark a section partial, which is about citations. The check sends nothing, so it is always on.

    It is forgiving about form and strict about precision. .61, 1204, 12 450, 45.2 million and 45% are found as 0.61, 1,204, 12,450, 45,200,000 and 0.45, and a field the writer was shown as 1e+05 backs “100,000”, but a figure is compared at the places it was written to, so “30%” is not a row’s 0.32 rounded. Totals of a numeric field over the cited rows, arithmetic shown in the sentence (“120 of 1,020 (11.8%)”, or “HR 0.78, a 22% lower hazard”), differences in points between two figures of one finding, years, counts of studies (“10 of the 12 were randomised trials”) and qualified figures (“about 1,200”, “c. 1,200”) are allowed. Ids written bare in prose (“studies 12 to 15”), significance thresholds (“p value below 0.05”, “at the 5% level”) and age decades (“in their 60s”) are not read as figures. A revision pass that writes a figure its draft did not have, in any form, is now discarded (gr_revision_new_figure), because the passes may not add anything.

  • gr_outline(alternatives =): more than one way to organise the review, compared by counting and chosen by you. gr_outline() made one call and handed back one grouping of the claims into sections. The grouping is the review’s argument, and a single proposal gave nothing to weigh it against. Asking again could not help: the default model takes no temperature, and the response cache answers an identical request with the reply it stored, so the second outline was the first.

    With alternatives = 3, each further outline is a request of its own, shown the groupings kept so far and asked to group the claims by a different organising principle. The first request is unchanged, so a run without alternatives sends the same request, caches the same way and still replays. Each alternative is verified as the first is. How far apart two outlines are is counted, not asked: the share of pairs of claims grouped together in one and apart in the other. One that groups the claims exactly as an earlier one did is dropped, as is one whose call failed or was cut off or none of whose sections held a claim once verified, and a warning (gr_outline_alternatives_short) says why. The first proposal comes back as before, with attr(, "comparison") laying the outlines side by side: sections, claims and contested claims per section, and distance from the first. No model picks the winner. gr_outline_pick() hands back the one you choose with its own claim assignment, and gr_synthesise(), its print method, its trace and gr_audit_report() say which outline the review was written from, unless you have since moved claims between its sections, which makes it an outline of your own (renaming its headings does not).

  • A cut pass that cut nothing is no longer kept as a cut. Every check gr_synthesise(coherence = ) made on a revision asked whether it was safe: the same studies cited, as often, on the same sentences, claiming no more than the draft did. None asked whether the pass had done its job, so a cut handed back as long as it went out (polished instead, returned as it was, or longer) passed them all and was reported as a kept cut. The cut pass must now return strictly fewer words of prose than the text it was given, or it is discarded with a gr_revision_uncut warning and a reason such as “the cut pass did not shorten the review: 812 words before, 815 after”. Headings, list markers and citation markers are not counted, so deleting a heading, turning a numbered list into bullets or writing three markers as a range is not a cut. The count is in words rather than tokens because a token count follows whichever tokenizer the session has set and moves with markup a reader never sees. There is no minimum: a tight draft may have nothing to lose but a filler phrase.

    The structure and register passes are not held to a length. A sentence-by-sentence polish of padded prose removed half its words while keeping every claim and hedge, more than a reply that dropped a whole section removed, so no bound could tell their job from cutting. Instead $coherence gains integer words_before and words_after columns, shown in the audit report’s table of revision passes, so a pass that halved the review can be seen.

  • .csv and .tsv are readable. An extractor claims them, so a folder of exported tables is read rather than skipped.

  • headers: reaching an endpoint that does not authenticate with a bearer token. base_url was enough only for a gateway that speaks the OpenAI shape and takes Authorization: Bearer, because that header was hardcoded. Most gateways standing in front of a company’s OpenAI and Anthropic tokens are somewhere else: Azure OpenAI authenticates with api-key, API Management adds a subscription key, and many want a cost-centre or correlation id. There was no way to express any of it.

    gr_client(headers = ) takes a named character vector, and gr_options(api_headers = ) sets one for every client, the form that belongs in a project’s .Rprofile. Two rules make it predictable. A header you name replaces the automatic Authorization rather than joining it, matched without regard to case, because HTTP field names are case-insensitive and curl is not: given both spellings it sends two headers and leaves the gateway to pick. And naming any header makes the API key optional, because nothing here can tell which of a stranger’s headers is the credential. NA as a value suppresses a header instead of sending it, which is how an OPENAI_API_KEY left set for another client in the same session is kept off the company gateway.

    The embeddings endpoint takes the same headers as the chat endpoint. They were two copies of the same three lines, which is how one of them ends up a release behind the other.

    Three things are refused rather than repaired. A name that is not a legal HTTP field name is a typo, not a header. A value carrying a control character is request splitting: CR/LF ends the header and starts one the caller never wrote, and these values come from environment variables and config files, which is exactly where a stray line ending comes from. And an empty value is refused because curl drops the header entirely, so c("api-key" = Sys.getenv("GATEWAY_KEY")) with that variable unset would otherwise leave without the credential and come back a 401 that looks like a wrong key rather than a missing one.

    Headers are excluded from the cache key, for the same reason the API key is: a rotating token or a per-request correlation id would make every lookup a miss. A header that changes which model answers belongs in base_url or model, where the cache can see it.

    gr_client() also prints now. It had no print method, so a client echoed at the console printed as a plain list with api_key in it, in full. Header values would have joined it there. Names are shown; values never are.

  • The claims protocol: a schema coded so studies can be compared, not only read. The first step of a claims-level synthesis, and the constraint it removes is the one everything downstream was capped by: a synthesis can only relate studies on dimensions the extraction table holds.

    evidence_table records the design “in the paper’s own words”, which is right for a table a person reads and wrong for one that gets crosstabbed: “RCT”, “randomised trial” and “randomized controlled trial” become three designs, so a gap analysis reports a design as absent while three of them sit in the table. So claims codes design and finding as enums and pairs each with the paper’s own wording (design_note, effect), which is the same bargain the evidence quotes already make for values: the coding can be checked rather than trusted. effect stays a string deliberately, because effect metrics are not commensurable across studies, and coercing “d = 0.42 (0.11, 0.73)” to a number is the shape of fault that turned “120 (60 per arm)” into 12060.

    Two fields the other templates lack, because they are what a synthesis argues from. measure is how the construct was measured, which is what surfaces the strongest thing a review can say: that a disagreement about effect size is a disagreement about measurement. limitation is the one the authors state, in their words, so it is quotable and therefore checkable, unlike a limitation a model infers.

    finding is coded relative to your question rather than to an intervention (supports / contradicts / mixed / no clear finding / not applicable), which is what lets a non-interventional literature have contradictions at all, and it is why an unedited template is now refused. A run could previously screen a whole corpus against “REPLACE: the population the review is about” and extract against “REPLACE THIS with your review question”, paying in full for a table framed by an instruction to supply the framing. gr_extract(), gr_screen() and gr_synthesise() now refuse a protocol whose question or criteria still begin with REPLACE, before anything is spent. The check is anchored on the whole word: there are real trials called REPLACE, and a review of one is not a template.

  • gr_claims(), gr_outline() and gr_gaps(): a review written from an argument instead of from rows. gr_synthesise()’s unit was the section, and sections came from an outline fixed before the reading; each was then drafted independently from the whole study table. Three things followed that no downstream editing could repair. The structure was the author’s hypothesis rather than a finding, and the strongest sentence a review contains is often structural. Studies arrived as rows, so the model wrote row by row: “Smith

    1. found X. Garcia (2022) found Y.” And nothing computed relations between studies, which is what synthesis is.

    gr_claims() turns the extraction table into statements about the literature, each naming the studies that support it, the studies that contradict it, and the field that distinguishes them. Every number is verified against the table, the check cited_ids() already makes on finished prose, moved one link earlier: an id that is not there is dropped and counted, a claim left with no supporting study is dropped entirely, and a moderator naming a column the table does not have is cleared, because an invented explanation for a real disagreement is the most convincing error this layer can make. $dropped records all of it, so a claims table that looks thin can be told from a literature that is.

    The study numbers are the ones gr_synthesise() cites, because both derive them from one function, and passing claims drawn from a different table is refused rather than trusted. Nothing downstream could detect that on its own: the numbers would all be valid and all mean other studies.

    gr_outline() derives the sections from the claims and hands them back as an ordinary outline you can accept or replace, verifying that every claim lands in exactly one section. gr_synthesise(claims = ) then gives each section its own claims and only the studies those claims rest on, ordered by breadth so a twelve-person pilot stops getting the same space as a two-thousand-person trial, and marks a section partial if it was handed a claim and did not write it up. gr_gaps() computes what the corpus does not contain (a declared category nobody studied, a dimension with no variation, an unreplicated claim, a disagreement nothing explains) in R, with no model call, so the gap list is a fact that can be checked by counting rather than an impression.

    The claims protocol from earlier in this release is the schema this wants as input, and gr_audit_report() gained a claims section so one document reads claim → studies → quotes → pages. Its new claims and records arguments come after all of 0.5.0’s, so a positional call written against 0.5.0 binds as it did.

    Ordering studies for emphasis deliberately does not rank designs. That would assert a cohort study beats a qualitative one, which is a methodological claim this package has no standing to make, and adding per-item scores into a total is what Cochrane says plainly is discouraged. Design is a grouping variable: what distinguishes the sides of a disagreement, and what gr_gaps() crosstabs. A principled weighting waits on an appraisal instrument.

  • Three revision passes, and a guard the citation check cannot make. A revision must not change the citations and must not arrive truncated. Both checks are necessary and neither is sufficient, because the most damaging thing an editing pass does leaves the citations exactly where they were. Editing for impact means deleting hedges, and the hedges are where the uncertainty lives: “three small trials suggest a modest benefit” comes back as “trials show a benefit”, same markers, same studies, a claim the evidence does not carry.

    So revision is three passes ("structure", "cut", "register"), each forbidden from doing the others’ job, each run on what survived the last, and each measured for escalation. A revision is discarded if it introduces a universal quantifier that was not there, uses a booster stem more often than the draft did, or carries fewer hedges than the draft’s rate implies.

    All three are matched on whole words, so “outcomes improved” is not the booster “prove”, and the hedge “unproven” is not a booster at all. Boosters are compared by count, not by which stems are present, so saying “demonstrates” three times where the draft said it once is introducing it.

    The hedge test scales with how much claim-bearing prose survived, so a shorter revision may carry fewer hedges, but never none if the draft had any. What it does not promise is that every legitimate cut passes: removing the most heavily hedged sentence lowers the rate and is refused, leaving the draft standing. Hedges and universals are measured on sentences carrying a citation; boosters on all the prose except headings, because uncited framing between the claims is where “the evidence demonstrates a clear benefit” actually gets written. coherence = TRUE runs all three; name them to run fewer. A draft too long to leave room for its own rewrite is skipped rather than sent.

  • iterative was cutting the wrong end of what it had gathered, and never fitted its final prompt at all. Two faults in the one reader that accumulates context across rounds.

    It pasted everything gathered and called gr_truncate_tokens() on the result, which keeps the head, so the chunks from the most recent round were the ones dropped. In a reader whose whole premise is “that did not answer it, go and get more”, it discarded the material it had just decided it needed. And it cut mid-chunk, which breaks the audit chain: a chunk cut in half no longer contains the sentence an answer quotes from it, so verified comes back false for a reason that has nothing to do with the document. Now it keeps whole chunks, ranked by the score that justified taking each one, so everything reaching the prompt is intact and still checkable.

    Worse, chunks_used and the evidence table were built from everything seen, including chunks truncation had removed from the prompt. The answer claimed support from text no model had been shown. Only what reached the prompt is reported now, notes$chunks_dropped says how much did not, and a run that dropped anything is partial.

    And the final answer call was never budgeted. Every other reader sizes its prompt to the context window; this one rendered everything gathered, so several rounds of top_k chunks went out over the window and the provider rejected the call after the entire loop had been paid for. When no gathered chunk fits one prompt, the loop stops and the reader returns NOT_IN_DOCUMENT marked partial.

  • The question is repeated at both ends of a long prompt. answer_messages() already asked last, which is the position that gets followed, but over several thousand tokens of excerpt an instruction that appears once at the bottom is a long way from the top. It now also appears before the body when the body is long enough to bury it, inside the existing message rather than as a new one so nothing indexing those positions shifts. The iterative step prompt and gr_synthesise()’s section prompt asked first and then handed over the bulk; both now ask again at the far end.

    restate is a [gr_read_spec()] setting ("auto", "always", "never") rather than a rule, because whether repeating the question helps is a question about a particular corpus and model. gr_compare() can take two recipes differing only in it and measure the difference, which is the honest way to settle it. The same goes for context_order = "edges", which has been in the package since 0.4 on the strength of a published finding and has never been measured here.

  • Every prompt is now budgeted against the prompt that is actually sent. The readers size their excerpts with gr_budget(overhead = ...), and parts of the prompts were not in that arithmetic: cite = TRUE sends a longer system prompt than cite = FALSE and every cited read budgeted for the short one, and the iterative step prompt adds 88 tokens of instruction to the answer system prompt and budgeted for the answer prompt alone. The prompt then overran the window by exactly the amount nobody counted, and the provider refused the call after the run had been paid for.

    The system prompt is now built once and used for both the budget and the call wherever the two could drift, and prompt_overhead() counts the question twice unless restatement is off, because the question is restated at the far end of a long prompt (above). Reserving room that goes unused costs a little context; under-reserving cost the answer.

  • Six connections between the stages of a review.

    The run has its own ceiling. gr_options(max_calls =) is per document by design (one enormous document must not starve the rest), and on its own that left the run unbounded: five documents under a 30-call ceiling made 125 calls, and the only corpus ceiling, max_total_usd, is unenforceable against a model with no registered price and is checked only after a document has been paid for. max_total_calls is checked before each document, so the overshoot is bounded by one document’s own ceiling. With neither ceiling set, the run now says once what its worst case is instead of leaving you to multiply.

    gr_synthesise() stops when the ceiling says so. One model call per section, and neither it nor the batched path checked trace_can_call(), so a run that had already spent its ceiling kept writing sections, one call each. A section the ceiling stops is marked partial and says why, rather than appearing as empty prose.

    A folder and its file list behave the same. gr_read_many(dir) skipped the files no extractor claims; gr_read_many(list.files(dir)) handed each of them to an extractor and recorded a failed row. Every pipeline uses the second form (gr_extract(screened$included) is a character vector), so the stage that reads the most documents was getting the worse behaviour. Both forms now skip those files and warn, as described above. The filter applies only when every element is a file that exists, so raw text, a mixed vector and a list() of sources are all untouched, and a gr_records still produces a failed row per unreadable file rather than dropping it. A record that was retrieved and could not be read is a fact a PRISMA count needs to keep. When the filter removes everything, the run aborts and says so.

    The search travels with the corpus it produced. gr_screening and gr_extraction carry the gr_records() they were run over, and gr_audit_report() picks it up, so the report’s search section and flow diagram do not depend on handing the same object over a second time. gr_extract() also takes the screening object itself, which is what carries the search across the hand-off: a character vector of paths cannot, so gr_extract(screened) keeps the search and the bibliographic fields while gr_extract(screened$included) keeps neither.

    A review can be one trace. gr_screen(), gr_extract() and gr_synthesise() take a trace =, so the stages of one review add up to one figure. Each used to start its own, and nothing said what the review cost.

    The argument is a parent, not the stage’s own counter, and that distinction is the whole design: a gr_trace is both the ledger of what a run did and the counter max_calls is measured against, and those want opposite things. Each stage runs on its own trace (so max_calls limits each stage as it always has, and each stage’s $trace reports that stage alone) and folds into the parent at the end, exactly as each document inside gr_read_many() does.
